March 20, 2026
To the Attention of; Hydro 2000 Inc and its Shareholders
Subject: Acquisition of 440 St. Philippe Street – Regulatory and Financial Assessment
At the request of Hydro 2000 Inc. (the “Hydro 2000”), Tandem Energy Services Inc.
(“TESI”), in its role as regulatory advisor, has reviewed the proposed acquisition of the
property located at 440 St. Philippe Street in Alfred, Ontario, including the associated
financing structure, planned capital improvements, and regulatory treatment.
Based on our review, it is our opinion that the proposed acquisition represents a
prudent and reasonable investment for Hydro 2000, both from a financial and
regulatory perspective.
Regulatory Considerations
Hydro 2000 operates within a cost-of-service regulatory framework under the Ontario
Energy Board. In practical terms, this means Hydro 2000 recovers its costs and earns
a regulated return through rates.
Only the portion of the building used for Hydro 2000 operations would be included in
rate base, (meaning the value of assets on which Hydro 2000 is permitted to earn that
regulated return). The residential leased portions of the building are considered non-
Hydro 2000 in nature and would be excluded.
Rental income generated from those non-Hydro 2000 portions would be recorded as
Other Revenue and applied as a revenue offset, reducing the overall revenue
requirement, or the amount Hydro 2000 needs to recover from customers through
rates.
This structure ensures that:
 ratepayers are not funding non-Hydro 2000 activities
 any benefit from those activities flows back to customers through lower rates.
Financial and Strategic Assessment
From a financial perspective, this is a straightforward shift from leasing to ownership.
Hydro 2000 is replacing an ongoing lease expense with control of a core operational
asset. The short-term financial impact is modest and can be absorbed within the
existing framework, particularly when considering the contribution of rental income,
which helps offset carrying costs and reduce pressure on rates.
Over time, Hydro 2000-use portion of the building can be incorporated into rate base,
supporting long-term financial stability. The additional rental unit further strengthens
the overall position, but the acquisition itself does not depend on it.
Shareholder Considerations
As the sole shareholder, the Municipality benefits through its ownership of Hydro 2000.
While the building is owned by Hydro 2000, it strengthens Hydro 2000 as a whole.
Hydro 2000 is effectively the entity that holds and manages the assets required to
deliver service. Adding a permanent operational facility, along with stable non-
regulated income, improves financial resilience, borrowing capacity, and overall
flexibility.
In practical terms:
 ratepayers benefit through reduced revenue requirements
 the Municipality benefits through a stronger, more valuable Hydro 2000.
Risk Considerations
TESI has considered the primary risks associated with the transaction. These are not
unusual for this type of investment and are well understood.
The key considerations are:
 Construction cost risk: The estimated $65,000 renovation cost is based on
current information and defined scope. As with any project, there is potential for
cost overruns; however, the magnitude is limited and can be absorbed within
Hydro 2000’s existing financial capacity.
 Rental risk: Rental income assumptions reflect current market conditions. There
is some exposure to vacancies or variability in rental rates over time, although
this risk is considered moderate and manageable.
2
 Regulatory treatment and allocation: This is not a risk to the viability of the
project, but it does require clear and consistent tracking. Hydro 2000 will need
to maintain appropriate allocation between Hydro 2000 and non-Hydro 2000
portions of the building to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements.
 Timing of rate recovery: The portion of the building attributable to Hydro 2000’s
operations will not be included in rate base, and therefore will not be reflected
in rates, until the next Cost of Service application (currently expected in 2030).
As a result, Hydro 2000 must absorb the carrying costs in the interim period.
In our view, these considerations are limited, well understood, and manageable. Hydro
2000 has sufficient financial capacity to absorb potential variability, and the proposed
structure appropriately addresses regulatory requirements. Importantly, the underlying
business case remains sound even without reliance on additional rental income.
Conclusion
In TESI’s opinion, the proposed acquisition of 440 St. Philippe Street is financially
sound, regulatorily compliant, and aligned with Hydro 2000’s obligation to manage its
assets in a prudent and cost-effective manner.
The transaction secures a critical operational asset, maintains rate stability in the near
term, and supports both long-term Hydro 2000 value and ratepayer benefit.
This approach is also consistent with a more conservative application of regulatory
principles than is sometimes observed in similar circumstances. By not seeking
immediate rate recovery and by ensuring that non-utility benefits flow through to
reduce the revenue requirement, Hydro 2000 has structured the transaction in a
manner that prioritizes ratepayer impact and minimizes regulatory risk.
Yours truly,
Manuela Ris, Regulatory Consultant
Tandem Energy Services Inc.

 Potential Municipal Equipment Operator Course
Recommended Motion:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Whereas municipal public works departments from across the Province of Ontario provide invaluable services to our communities ensuring the health and safety of all residents;
And Whereas if it was not for our municipal public works employees from across the Province of Ontario maintaining our public roads systems, our communities would not be able to function as emergency personnel could not respond to calls, school buses could not get our children to school, residents would not be able to get to work, school or appointments and many more basic functions would not be able to happen;
And Whereas municipal public works departments are already feeling the impacts of a labour shortage, which will only be exasperated over the next three to five years, which will cause levels of service municipalities are able to provide to ensure the health and safety of our residents to decrease;
And Whereas there is currently no provincial-wide course that properly trains potential municipal public works employees, specifically relating to municipal heavy equipment.
Therefore It Be Resolved that the Township of Amaranth supports the work of the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors to develop a Municipal Equipment Operator Course to address this issue;
And That the Township of Amaranth calls on the Province of Ontario’s Ministry of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades to fully fund the Municipal Equipment Operator Course in 2024 through the Skills Development Fund;
And That a copy of this resolution be sent to the Minister of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades David Piccinni, the Township of Amaranth’s Member of Provincial Parliament Sylvia Jones and the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors.

Recommended Motion:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Whereas current provincial-municipal fiscal arrangements are undermining Ontario’s economic prosperity and quality of life;
Whereas nearly a third of municipal spending in Ontario is for services in areas of provincial responsibility and expenditures are outpacing provincial contributions by nearly $4 billion a year;
Whereas municipal revenues, such as property taxes, do not grow with the economy or inflation;
Whereas unprecedented population and housing growth will require significant investments in municipal infrastructure;
Whereas municipalities are being asked to take on complex health and social challenges – like homelessness, supporting asylum seekers and addressing the mental health and addictions crises;
Whereas inflation, rising interest rates, and provincial policy decisions are sharply constraining municipal fiscal capacity;
Whereas property taxpayers – including people on fixed incomes and small businesses – can’t afford to subsidize income re-distribution programs for those most in need;
Whereas the province can, and should, invest more in the prosperity of communities;
Whereas municipalities and the provincial government have a strong history of collaboration;
Therefore, Be It Resolved That the Province of Ontario commit to undertaking with the Association of Municipalities of Ontario a comprehensive social and economic prosperity review to promote the stability and sustainability of municipal finances across Ontario;
And That a letter be sent to request advocacy in advance of the Provincial budget to the Premier, the Dufferin-Caledon MPP and local municipalities.

August 28, 2026
Town of Amherstburg

Attention: Sydnee Botham, Development Engineering Coordinator
Re: Coulson McLeod Severances
Letter of Conformance, Maintenance Period Commencement, Securities Reduction and Building
Permits
Dear Sydnee,
We are the consulting engineers for the above-noted development. In accordance with the approved
engineering drawings and applicable municipal requirements, we have reviewed the completed
servicing and site works associated with the severances.
A final site inspection was conducted on August 11, 2026 with representatives of the Owner,
Contractor and Municipality. Based on our review of the completed works, construction records,
and site inspection, the works have been substantially completed in general accordance with the
approved engineering drawings and specifications.
1.0 As-Constructed Works and Conformance
An as-constructed drawing package has been prepared and submitted to the Municipality for
review. The package documents the servicing, roadway, grading and other works constructed as
part of the development.
Based on our review, the completed works are in general conformance with the approved
engineering drawings and applicable municipal requirements.
The individual lot grading shown within the as-constructed drawing package remains proposed, as
final lot grading within the individual lots will be completed in conjunction with future residential
construction. The roadway and other works within the municipal right-of-way have been
constructed and are represented based on available as-constructed survey information.
2.0 Outstanding Deficiencies
The following minor deficiencies were identified during the final site inspection:
• Installation of two manhole ladder rungs;
• Parging of catchbasins; and
• Completion of topsoil and seeding.
These items are considered minor in nature and do not affect the general functionality of the
completed servicing infrastructure. The Contractor has been advised of the outstanding items and
is responsible for their completion.
A follow-up inspection will be undertaken, as required, to confirm that the deficiencies have been
satisfactorily addressed.
3.0 Value of Completed and Outstanding Works
The total contract value for the servicing works is approximately $410,000. Based on our review,
the majority of the contracted works have been completed. The estimated value of the remaining
outstanding works is summarized below:
Outstanding Item Estimated Value
Installation of two (2) manhole ladder rungs $800
Parging of catchbasins $1,000
Topsoil and seeding $5,500
Total Estimated Outstanding Works $7,300
The above values are provided for the Municipality's consideration in determining the appropriate
reduction in the Developer's securities in accordance with the applicable development/severance
agreement and municipal requirements.
4.0 Maintenance Period
Based on our review of the completed works and the final site inspection conducted on August 11,
2026, it is our opinion that the works had achieved substantial completion as of that date.
Accordingly, we recommend that the maintenance period commence effective August 11, 2026.
The minor deficiencies identified during the final inspection, as noted in Section 2 of this letter,
do not prevent the works from being considered substantially complete and are to be completed
by the Contractor during the applicable maintenance period.
The maintenance period shall be administered in accordance with the requirements of the
applicable development/severance agreement and Municipal standards.
5.0 Reduction in Developer's Securities
Based on the substantial completion of the servicing works, the submitted as-constructed drawing
package, and our review of the completed works, we recommend that the Municipality proceed
with a reduction in the Developer's securities. The specific amount of the reduction is to be
determined in accordance with the applicable development/severance agreement and Municipal
requirements.
The total contract value for the servicing works is approximately $410,000. The estimated value
of the remaining outstanding works is approximately $7,300, as summarized in Section 3 of this
letter.
6.0 Building Permits
The servicing and roadway works required to support the development have been substantially
completed and the development is adequately serviced.
Accordingly, we recommend that the Municipality proceed with the issuance of full building
permits for the individual lots, subject to completion of any remaining municipal requirements and
applicable conditions.
The outstanding deficiencies identified above are minor in nature and do not affect the ability of
the individual lots to proceed with residential building construction.
7.0 Recommendation
Based on the foregoing, we recommend that the Municipality:
1. Accept the submitted as-constructed drawing package for the purposes of documenting the
completed works;
2. Recognize the servicing works as substantially complete, subject to completion of the
minor outstanding deficiencies;
3. Recognize August 11, 2026 as the commencement date of the maintenance period, based
on the determination that substantial completion was achieved as of that date, with the
outstanding minor deficiencies to be completed by the Contractor during the applicable
maintenance period;
4. Proceed with the applicable reduction in the Developer's securities in accordance with the
development/severance agreement and municipal requirements; and
5. Permit the issuance of full building permits for the individual lots, subject to the
Municipality's remaining requirements.
Please contact the undersigned should you require any additional information or documentation in
support of the above recommendations.
Sincerely,

EXPLANATORY NOTE
Protective Services Department
By-Law Number: 3866-2026
Date: September 14, 2026
From: Chad Belanger, Municipal Enforcement Officer
Subject: Administrative Monetary Penalty System (AMPS)
RECOMMENDATION
THAT By-Law Numbered 3866-2026 being a By-Law to implement an Administrative
Monetary Penalty System to regulate and enforce designated By-Laws in the Township
of Augusta, be read a first time, a second time, a third time, and be enacted as read.
BACKGROUND/EXPLANATION
Municipalities face significant challenges in ensuring By-Law compliance while
balancing the demands on judicial resources and municipal budgets. The Administrative
Monetary Penalty System (AMPS) program provides a modern solution by allowing for
direct municipal oversight of minor By-Law infractions. This approach not only
accelerates the resolution process but also enhances local governance.
The Township of Augusta currently utilizes the Provincial Offences Act (POA) system to
prosecute its existing By-Laws. However, the Township is now exploring the
enforcement of parking violations, which, under provincial mandate, must be processed
through the Administrative Monetary Penalty System.
This shift would result in the use of two separate systems for By-Law enforcement: the
POA for general By-Law infractions and AMPS for parking violations. It is important to
note that the POA is structured to address three categories of offences: Part I (minor
offences), Part II (parking offences), and Part III (more serious offences requiring a
court appearance). With the mandated transition to AMPS for parking, Part II offences
would no longer be processed under the POA system.
While we are currently exploring a transition to the Administrative Monetary Penalty
System, doing so would significantly enhance our enforcement options. Under AMPS,
standard Part I penalty notices can be handled through an efficient, internal
administrative process. However, adopting AMPS does not strip away traditional
enforcement pathways—we will retain full authority to initiate Part III proceedings
through the Provincial Offences Act (POA) court system for repeat offenders or severe
cases where AMPS does not achieve compliance. Ideally, AMPS will resolve most
minor infractions quickly and collaboratively, while the courts remain available as a firm
recourse when necessary.
The Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, as amended, along with Ontario Regulation
333/07: Administrative Penalties, grants municipalities the authority to implement AMPS
for the efficient enforcement, processing, and adjunction of By-Law infractions. This
framework is designed to bolster municipalities in ensuring adherence to their By-Laws
by substantially shortening the dispute resolution timeframe. By adopting AMPS, the
municipality takes on full responsibility for managing and prosecuting violations,
encompassing the processing of payments and the recovery of penalties. This shift not
only streamlines enforcement procedures but also enhances the municipality’s capacity
to maintain order and compliance within the community.
Should an infraction notice issued under the AMPS Penalty System remain unpaid, the
Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, as amended, empowers the municipality to add
the outstanding AMPS Penalty to the offender’s property tax roll, enabling its collection
in the same manner as Township taxes. In instances where adding the AMPS penalty to
the tax roll is not possible, the municipality has the option to engage a collection agency
to facilitate the recovery of a portion of the penalty. This ensures a flexible yet effective
approach to enforcing compliance and securing penalty payments.
Municipalities are in constant pursuit of strategies that are both efficient and effective in
enforcing compliance with By-Laws. Although the traditional court system serves its
purpose, it often results in lengthy processes and incurs significant costs for both the
municipality and individuals accused of infractions. In response, AMPS emerges as an
innovative solution designed to streamline enforcement procedures. By adopting AMPS,
municipalities can expedite dispute resolutions, significantly reduce legal expenditures,
and alleviate the caseload burden on the judicial system. This method not only benefits
the local government by enhancing operational efficiency and potentially increasing
revenue through fines but also offers residents a quicker, more direct way to resolve
violations.
Furthermore, it contributes to the overall effectiveness of the judicial system to allow
courts to focus on resources on more pressing matters, thereby improving access to
justice for all citizens. Under the traditional system, appealing a notice means taking an
entire day off to wait in court for your case to come up. With AMPS, you are given an
exact date and time for your review, saving you time and avoiding unnecessary waiting.
To date, the Administrative Monetary Penalty System (AMPS) has been adopted by the
municipalities of Prescott, North Grenville, Merrickville-Wolford, and the Township of
Leeds and the Thousand Islands. Brockville and Elizabethtown-Kitley continue to
monitor the framework for potential future consideration, but neither is actively
transitioning to AMPS at present.
Benefits to the Municipality:
1. Efficiency in Enforcement
AMPS allows for quicker resolution of By-Law infractions, reducing the burden on the
court system and enabling faster corrective action from violators.
2. Financial Advantages
The system is designed to be cost-effective, reducing the need for extensive legal
proceedings and potentially generating additional revenue from the penalties, which can
be reinvested into Township services. All revenue from fines stays within the Township
unlike the traditional POA System.
3. Enhanced Compliance
The immediacy and simplicity of the AMPS process encourage higher rates of
compliance, contributing to a safer and more orderly community.
4. Community Engagement
Implementing AMPS demonstrates a Township’s commitment to proactive governance
and community standards, enhancing public trust and engagement.
5. Customizable Framework
AMPS provides Townships with the flexibility to set fines and penalties based on local
needs and priorities, ensuring a tailored approach to By-Law enforcement.
Township staff will be required to manage the requirements of AMPs. This includes the
following:
• Financial duties include payment tracking and reporting paid infraction notices
directly to the Protective Services Department.
• Duties of Screening Officers assigned to existing staff
• The Manager of Protective Services will assume additional operational oversight
and administration of the AMPS Program
• Conduct updates to the website for proper administration of AMPS
• Social media campaigns to inform the public
• Updating current By-Laws for implementing AMPS

a pecuniary interest in a matter that was discussed at a meeting of Council or a Committee of Council,

Member had a pecuniary interest in a matter for which they were disqualified to debate or vote, OR
the individual may bring an application to court to have a judge determine whether the Member had a
pecuniary interest in the matter at Council and, as a result, should have declared that interest under
the MCIA and not participated in the debate or vote.
In both avenues for lodging a complaint, the individual must bring forward the complaint within six
weeks of the alleged violation having occurred.
The Integrity Commissioner does not have authority to commence an “own motion” investigation and

Introduction
This is the City of Belleville’s Community Safety
and Well-Being (CSWB) Plan for 2026 through
2030.
CSWB plans aim to enhance the safety, health,
and well-being of communities by addressing
the root causes of crime, disorder, and poor
health outcomes. They bring together partners
across sectors to identify key risks and
coordinate actions that support prevention,
early intervention, and improved outcomes for
residents.
CSWB plans are mandated under Part XVI of the
Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019 (CSPA),
which requires municipalities to develop and
review their plans every four years. This plan will
guide local CSWB efforts in Belleville over the
2026–2030 period.
This work is grounded in collaboration. Input
from service providers, community
organizations, and residents helped identify the
most significant risks facing the community and
the areas where coordinated action can have the
greatest impact.
This plan focuses on three priority areas:
• Housing and Homelessness
• Mental Health and Addiction
• Access to Services and Supports
While no single plan can address all community
challenges, it provides a framework for
coordinated, sustainable action. The strategies
outlined in this document are intended to
support ongoing efforts, strengthen
partnerships, and contribute to improved
community safety and well-being over time.

The City of Belleville’s 2026–2030 Community Safety and Well-Being (CSWB) plan outlines a
coordinated, collaborative approach to addressing key factors that influence the safety and well-
being of residents, aligned with Ontario’s Community Safety and Well-Being Planning Framework.
This plan reflects input from residents, service providers, and community partners, and builds on
existing strategies and initiatives. It focuses on shared priorities and opportunities where
coordinated action can help strengthen outcomes and support a safer, healthier, and more
connected community.
While a range of ideas and priorities were identified through engagement, this plan focuses on three
aligned strategies, detailed in the sections that follow.
This plan reflects input from residents, service providers, and community partners, supported by
local data and reports.

• Review of local reports and data
Together, these inputs helped identify shared priorities and opportunities for coordinated action.
Implementation is supported through a shared leadership approach. Strategy leads help advance
each priority in collaboration with partners, while the Advisory Committee provides subject matter
expertise and supports alignment across initiatives. A Governance Committee provides oversight
and serves as a link to Council, which remains ultimately accountable. Progress is monitored over
time through regular updates, shared learning, and ongoing use of data to support coordination and
continuous improvement.

Understanding Our Community
To understand what is shaping safety and well-being
in Belleville, this plan brings together local
information, including from the Belleville Police
Service and community data sources. Taken together,
the voices and the data help tell a shared story about
who we are, what is changing, and where partners can
focus to reduce harm and strengthen well-being.
Belleville is a growing community. According to the
2021 Statistics Canada Census, Belleville’s population
was 55,071—up 8.6% from 2016.i As the city grows and
changes, CSWB planning helps local partners
anticipate pressures and strengthen the supports that
help people stay housed, well, and connected to
services.
Some community characteristics are best understood
across the wider Belleville–Quinte West area (the
census metropolitan area), which reflects where many
people live, work, and access services.
Across the Belleville–Quinte West area, people bring a
range of cultures, identities, and lived experiences to
community life. In the 2021 Census, 5.2% of residents
identified as First Nations, Métis, or Inuit, higher than
Ontario overall (2.8%). The immigrant population was
8.3% (lower than Ontario at 29.1%), and 4.1% of
residents identified as part of a racialized group (lower
than Ontario at 29.3%). These differences are
important to consider through a CSWB lens: they
remind local partners to design supports that are
welcoming and culturally safe, and to work with
Indigenous partners and diverse communities so
services are accessible, respectful, and responsive.

Please be advised that at its meeting held on June 22, 2026, the Council of the Town of
Whitby adopted the following as Resolution # 166-26:
Whereas local councils are elected by residents to make planning decisions that
reflect the needs and priorities of their communities;
Whereas municipalities rely on extensive public consultation, professional
planning advice, engineering studies, and technical reports when making land-
use decisions;
Whereas the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT) has the authority to overturn municipal
planning decisions, often requiring municipalities to spend significant taxpayer
dollars defending decisions that have already undergone a thorough local review
process;
Whereas lengthy and costly appeals can delay housing projects, consume
municipal resources, and reduce the ability of municipalities to focus on
delivering services to residents; and,
Whereas local governments should have greater certainty and authority when
decisions are consistent with approved Official Plans, provincial policies, and
sound planning principles.

Report Summary
The purpose of this report is to obtain approval by Committee to adjust and/or write-off
the balance of various tax accounts as set out in the attached Appendix A. Total
adjustments are $154,891.11, including $49,495.45 in City of Brampton taxes. These
adjustments are a normal and recurring component of the City’s annual tax write-off
provision, are accounted for within the approved budget, and have no impact on the
overall tax levy.
Background
Sections 334, 354, 357 and 358 of the Municipal Act, 2001 provide the authorities and
reasons for the write-off, cancellation, reduction or refund of taxes.
Current Situation
The total tax amount to be cancelled is $154,891.11. The total amount will be allocated
as follows:
City of Brampton: $ 49,495.45

Background
Response Times Defined
Response times are defined by the Canadian Triage Acuity Score (CTAS), a commonly used
system that prioritizes patient care based on severity, signs and symptoms.
The Canadian Triage and Acuity Score has five levels:
*CTAS-1- Resuscitation: conditions that are considered threats to life or limb or have an
imminent risk of deterioration requiring immediate aggressive intervention.
*CTAS-2- Emergent: conditions that are a potential threat to life, limb or function requiring
rapid medical interventions, and the use of condition specific controlled medical acts.
*CTAS-3- Urgent: conditions that could potentially progress to a serious problem requiring
emergency interventions.
*CTAS-4- Less Urgent: conditions that relate to patient age, distress, potential for
deterioration or complications that would benefit from intervention or reassurance.
*CTAS-5- Non-Urgent: conditions that may be acute but non-urgent as well as conditions
which may be part of a chronic problem with or without evidence of deterioration.
* Sudden Cardiac Arrest (SCA): defined as vital signs absent.
Response Time Targets & Approval Authorities
Response time standards for Sudden Cardiac Arrest (SCA) and CTAS 1 are established by
the Ministry of Health, while response time targets are approved by Council. Response time
targets for CTAS 2 through CTAS 5 are developed by Brant-Brantford Paramedic Services
(BBPS) and approved by Council. In accordance with legislative requirements, BBPS submits
an annual report to Committee and Council for review and approval of response time targets.
Response Time Targets Defined

Plan in Minutes refers to the time from when dispatch receives a call to the arrival of a BBPS
paramedic for CTAS 1 thorough 5 calls. For SCA incidents, it refers to the time from call receipt
by dispatch to the arrival of the first trained / qualified responder capable of providing
defibrillation.
Plan in % is the target percentage of times that the plan in minutes will be met.
Performance in % is the actual percentage of times that the plan in minutes was met.

PGO Governance Briefing No. 1
Integrity Begins with Governance
Understanding the Inspector General's Vision for Police Governance
The recent announcement of a province-wide Police Integrity and Anti-Corruption Inspection has
understandably generated considerable discussion among municipal police service boards.
While the inspection has received significant attention, the Inspector General's Annual Report
demonstrates that it is part of a much broader vision for policing oversight in Ontario.
Throughout the report, three themes are consistently linked:
 Integrity
 Legitimacy
 Public Confidence
The report makes it clear that public confidence is not determined solely by the actions of individual
police officers. It is also influenced by leadership, governance, transparency, accountability and the
systems that guide decision-making throughout the policing sector. Strong governance is presented as a
critical contributor to legitimate policing and enduring public trust.
This is an important message for every police service board.
Integrity does not begin when an inspection is announced.
It begins with the governance framework a board establishes, the questions it asks, the policies it
adopts, the oversight it exercises, and the culture of accountability and continuous improvement it
promotes.
What Does This Mean for Municipal Police Service Boards?
For municipal police service boards, the recently announced Integrity and Anti-Corruption Inspection
should be viewed within the broader context of the Inspector General's oversight philosophy.
2
The inspection is intended to assess whether governance systems are in place to prevent, detect and
respond to integrity risks—not simply whether misconduct has occurred.
Boards should consider whether their governance framework demonstrates effective oversight through
current policies, meaningful reporting, clear accountability, regular governance review and a
commitment to continuous improvement.
What Does This Mean for OPP Detachment Boards?
Although OPP Detachment Boards do not govern stand-alone police services, the broader governance
themes identified throughout the Annual Report are equally relevant.
The principles of legitimacy, accountability, transparency, evidence-informed decision-making and
continuous improvement apply across Ontario's policing governance framework.
For OPP Detachment Boards, these themes reinforce the importance of effective governance through
informed oversight of detachment performance, meaningful engagement with the communities they
serve, thoughtful strategic discussions and ongoing board development.
While the current integrity inspection is focused on municipal police services and boards, the
governance principles underpinning the Inspector General's work apply across the policing sector and
should inform every board's approach to governance.

 What governance improvements should our board prioritize over the next 12 months and how do
we ensure continuity and focus after the coming municipal elections?

Amendment to Noise By-law - Councillor Caputo
 WHEREAS excessive noise has the effect of interfering with the use and enjoyment of an individual’s property; and
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, 2001 authorizes municipalities to pass by laws regulating noise and other related nuisances in order to protect the health, safety, and well-being of persons, and the quiet enjoyment of property; and
WHEREAS residents are increasingly entertaining at home, including hosting backyard gatherings and outdoor social events, resulting in growing concerns regarding late-evening noise impacts on surrounding neighbourhoods; and
WHEREAS City events including live band concerts and sports events with loudspeakers, result in noise disturbance; and
WHEREAS the City seeks to balance reasonable residential enjoyment with the need to protect adjacent property owners from undue noise disturbances.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Staff BE DIRECTED to prepare an amendment to the Noise By-law to establish a maximum permitted noise level of less than 50 decibels after 11:00 p.m., applicable to all residential properties, including but not limited to noise generated from outdoor entertainment, backyard events, concerts, sporting events, amplified sound, musical instruments, or other sound-producing devices; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to conduct a review of noise by-laws and decibel limits in other Ontario municipalities, including but not limited to comparable urban and suburban cities, and report back on best practices, enforcement models, and recommended alignment opportunities; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to place the proposed Noise By-law amendment on a future Council agenda for consideration, accompanied by a report summarizing findings from the municipal comparator review and outlining any operational or enforcement implications.

What these numbers mean as population
Whatever the reconciled figure turns out to be, the scale is significant against Brockton’s existing base. The 2021
Census recorded 4,030 households in Brockton, at an average of roughly 2.4 people per household.
• The 433-unit Housing Accelerator Fund commitment alone represents an increase of about 10.7% in
Brockton’s total dwellings — on the order of 1,000 additional residents — within a three-year window.
• The Eastridge developments already built, under construction, or committed — roughly 211 units across the
three projects listed above — represent about 5% of Brockton’s entire housing stock, concentrated in a single
corner of one town.
• Brockton’s population grew 3.4% in the five years between the 2016 and 2021 censuses. The current
commitments imply a rate several times that, sustained.
This growth is not distributed across the municipality. It is concentrated in Walkerton, which is also where the
hospital, the emergency department, the birthing centre and the surgical program are located.
These are order-of-magnitude figures based on census averages, and I would welcome staff correcting them with
better data. That is part of the point: the Municipality has this information and residents do not.
The hospital is already operating in a fragile state
This is not a hypothetical future strain. Emergency department service within the hospital corporation —
including in Walkerton — has been repeatedly interrupted by staffing shortages, and remains reduced across the
corporation today:
• At a special meeting on December 17, 2021, the SBGHC Board of Directors approved a reduction of services.
Effective December 27, 2021, the Walkerton hospital emergency department was closed overnight, from 8:00
PM to 8:00 AM, for what the hospital described as an indefinite period. It remained on reduced hours until
the site was returned to full service in the spring of 2022 — roughly six months. The Chesley inpatient unit
was simultaneously converted to a 20-bed Alternate Level of Care unit to permit a staffing model requiring
fewer registered nurses.
• The Walkerton emergency department closed overnight again on September 30 and October 1, 2022, due to
shortages of both RNs and RPNs, with ambulance bypass in effect. Further temporary closures affecting
Walkerton were announced in August 2023.
• The Chesley emergency department has operated on reduced hours since September 2019. It was fully closed
for eight weeks from October 7 to December 2, 2022, and has since operated weekday daytime hours only.
• The Durham site recorded 96 short-notice emergency department closures in the 2023/24 fiscal year
alone, which the hospital cited as the reason for removing all ten of its inpatient beds in June 2024.
• The Chesley and Durham emergency departments remain on reduced hours today, a situation acknowledged
at the hospital’s June 2026 annual meeting. The hospital reported in 2022/23 that staffing was heavily reliant
on agency nurses and that no increase in service could be anticipated; agency staffing costs were still being
reported as a challenge to the board in late 2025.
In reducing Walkerton’s emergency hours, the Board’s stated rationale included that five alternate 24/7
emergency departments were available within 51 kilometres.
The nearest of those alternatives is not holding capacity in reserve. Hanover & District Hospital — the closest 24/7
emergency department to Walkerton — reported 17,662 emergency visits, 1,091 admitted patients, 1,672 surgeries
and 166 births in 2025/26, in a 28-bed hospital. That is roughly 3,200 more emergency visits than the Walkerton
site handled in the same year. Hanover has described itself as the second busiest emergency department in the
Grey-Bruce region. In early 2023 it reported emergency volumes up 19.8% year over year and 35% above pre-
pandemic levels, with patient acuity up 21.2% year over year and nearly 40% above pre-pandemic levels. Its
2025/26 annual report publishes raw volumes but no year-over-year comparison, no baseline, and no acuity data,
so the current trend is not on the public record. Hanover continues to issue public notices about high patient
volumes and extended wait times, noting that patients waiting for inpatient beds limit its capacity to see new
arrivals.
One structural point should not be overlooked. In its 2025/26 annual report, Hanover & District Hospital states
plainly that rural hospitals are globally funded by the Ministry of Health, that the hospital must work within that
fixed amount regardless of its volumes, and that higher volumes do not result in more funding for patient care.
Hanover finished that year with a deficit of $1,534 on $29.4 million in revenue — effectively no margin at all. The
assumption that population growth will bring proportionate health service capacity with it is not supported by
how these hospitals are actually funded.
A hospital that has closed its Walkerton emergency department overnight for six months, and repeatedly since,
for want of nursing staff is not a service holding spare capacity in reserve for a thousand new residents.
The hospital is not planning for this growth
South Bruce Grey Health Centre released its Strategic Plan 2026–2030 in October 2025. The plan contains no
population growth assumption. Its environmental scan relies on 2021 census data. It makes no reference to the
Ministerial Zoning Order, the Housing Accelerator Fund commitment, or any projected increase in the population
it serves.
The plan sets out 60 acute care beds organization-wide, of which 20 are at Walkerton. It proposes no increase. It
describes emergency volumes as consistent over the past ten years and births as steady between 400 and 450
annually. Expanded services appear in the plan only as something the community requested — not as a
commitment. The plan also notes that Alternate Level of Care rates are high across all sites, meaning a share of
those 60 beds is occupied by patients awaiting long-term care rather than receiving acute care.
3. Publish staff’s projected population for Brockton at the completion of these commitments, and the
assumptions behind it.
4. Formally write to South Bruce Grey Health Centre and to Ontario Health, on the record, advising them
of Brockton’s committed housing growth and the growth advertised by neighbouring municipalities,
requesting confirmation of how the hospital intends to serve the resulting population, and requesting current
emergency volume and patient acuity trend data.
5. Report publicly on whether hospital, emergency and primary care capacity has been considered in
Brockton’s growth planning to date, and if so, in which documents.
6. Before entering into further growth commitments, undertake a municipality-wide public consultation on
the cumulative rate and scale of growth Brockton is pursuing, and report on whether residents support
proceeding on that basis.
On item 6, I want to be precise about what I am asking for, because I anticipate the response that consultation has
already occurred. Brockton has held statutory public meetings under the Planning Act, and engagement was
undertaken in connection with the Ministerial Zoning Order and the Housing Accelerator Fund action plan. Those
processes were each tied to a single instrument or a single application, and none of them asked residents about
the combined effect of all of these commitments taken together.
What has never been put to this community is the whole picture at once: the reconciled total number of units
Brockton is committed to, the population that implies, the concentration of that growth in Walkerton, and the
state of the hospital, emergency and primary care capacity that must serve it. A consultation that satisfies this
request would be actively promoted to all residents of the Municipality, would present that information together
in advance, would be about the overall rate and scale of growth rather than about any individual application, and
would report publicly on what residents said. Meetings already held do not meet that description, and I would ask
that Council not treat them as having done so.
So that these requests are actionable rather than open-ended, I ask that Council direct staff to report back on
items 1 through 5 at the first regular meeting of Council in October 2026. The underlying information
already exists in the Municipality’s records; publishing it should not require an extended study.
I am asking that these questions be answered before further growth commitments are made, not after. Brockton
has entered into significant obligations — a federal funding agreement, a provincial zoning order, and the
disposition of municipal land — without publishing what they add up to, and without establishing that the
residents of this community support growth at this scale and pace. Council should satisfy itself of that support,
through a genuine public process, before the plan proceeds further.
I would be pleased to appear as a delegation should Council wish to discuss this further.
Respectfully submitted,
Darren Holm
Walkerton, Ontario

Authorization
This report is being prepared in response to an appointment by the Municipality of
Brockton, dated February 8, 2022, to investigate drainage issues on the properties of the
petitioning property owners, in accordance with Section 4 of the Drainage Act, R.S.O.

Objective & Recommendations
The objective of this report is to determine a drainage solution to help alleviate ponding,
provide a subsurface drainage outlet, and improve the quality of the stormwater for the
properties in the watershed.
This report recommends the construction of a new Main Drain beginning at Lot 16,
Concession 11, proceeding to Lot 20, Concession 13, and a new Branch ‘A’ Drain
beginning at Lot 18, Concession 11, proceeding to Lot 19, Concession 11, Municipality
of Brockton (Geographic Township of Greenock), Bruce County.

Speak at a Meeting
Menu
The City of Burlington relies on our residents to make sure we're representing the interests of the community. Speaking at a Standing Committee or Council meeting is a great way to keep us informed and accountable to your needs.
Register to speak at a meeting
Register to speak at a meeting
You can register to speak at a meeting by completing our delegation registration form
Registration deadline - You must register by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, you must register by noon on the Friday before the meeting. At the meeting, delegations are heard in the order that we receive them.
If you do not wish to speak, but would like to submit your comments in writing, please email your comments to Legislative Services. Written correspondence will be circulated to Committee members prior to the meeting.
Presentations and handouts
PowerPoint presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon on the Friday before the meeting. 
Presentation tips
Here are some helpful tips on how you can prepare for your presentation.
Make notes or write out the text of your presentation. Written material will help you to keep focused and stay within the presentation time limit
Larger groups should select a spokesperson to make their presentation. If you are appearing on behalf of a larger group, such as a neighbourhood group, let the clerk know in advance
Meeting process
This is how meetings typically run and what you can expect:
Delegations are heard shortly after the start of the meeting. The committee Chair or Mayor at Council will call out your name and identify the subject matter that you will be speaking about. You will also be reminded of the delegation speaking time limit of 10 minutes at committee and five minutes at council. Please address your remarks to the Chair and Members of the Committee, or if you are at Council, to the Mayor and Members of Council
After you are done speaking, the Chair or the Mayor at Council will ask members of Council if they have any questions for you
Once all questions have been asked, the Chair or Mayor at Council will thank you for your remarks and will not entertain any more comments from your delegation
Once all delegations have been heard, the committee will discuss each agenda item in the order of the approved agenda. Committee members will discuss and debate each item and form a recommendation, which will be forwarded to Council for final approval. In-person delegates may remain in the Council Chambers or leave to watch a livestream of the meeting online.
If you have delegated at Committee and want to speak at Council as a delegation, you must only present new information. All seven Council members are members of the standing committees, so they will have heard your delegation at committee. If the matter you want to speak to is on the Council agenda, you may register as a delegation up to noon the day before the Council meeting
For information on the rules and order of delegations at standing committee and Council meetings, please refer to our Consolidated Procedure Bylaw (059-2024).
Give us your feedback
After speaking at a committee or Council meeting, please take a few minutes to give us your feedback  on the process of registering and delegating.

Speak at a Meeting
Menu
The City of Burlington relies on our residents to make sure we're representing the interests of the community. Speaking at a Standing Committee or Council meeting is a great way to keep us informed and accountable to your needs.
Register to speak at a meeting
Register to speak at a meeting
You can register to speak at a meeting by completing our delegation registration form
Registration deadline - You must register by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, you must register by noon on the Friday before the meeting. At the meeting, delegations are heard in the order that we receive them.
If you do not wish to speak, but would like to submit your comments in writing, please email your comments to Legislative Services. Written correspondence will be circulated to Committee members prior to the meeting.
Presentations and handouts
PowerPoint presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon on the Friday before the meeting. 
Presentation tips
Here are some helpful tips on how you can prepare for your presentation.
Make notes or write out the text of your presentation. Written material will help you to keep focused and stay within the presentation time limit
Larger groups should select a spokesperson to make their presentation. If you are appearing on behalf of a larger group, such as a neighbourhood group, let the clerk know in advance
Meeting process
This is how meetings typically run and what you can expect:
Delegations are heard shortly after the start of the meeting. The committee Chair or Mayor at Council will call out your name and identify the subject matter that you will be speaking about. You will also be reminded of the delegation speaking time limit of 10 minutes at committee and five minutes at council. Please address your remarks to the Chair and Members of the Committee, or if you are at Council, to the Mayor and Members of Council
After you are done speaking, the Chair or the Mayor at Council will ask members of Council if they have any questions for you
Once all questions have been asked, the Chair or Mayor at Council will thank you for your remarks and will not entertain any more comments from your delegation
Once all delegations have been heard, the committee will discuss each agenda item in the order of the approved agenda. Committee members will discuss and debate each item and form a recommendation, which will be forwarded to Council for final approval. In-person delegates may remain in the Council Chambers or leave to watch a livestream of the meeting online.
If you have delegated at Committee and want to speak at Council as a delegation, you must only present new information. All seven Council members are members of the standing committees, so they will have heard your delegation at committee. If the matter you want to speak to is on the Council agenda, you may register as a delegation up to noon the day before the Council meeting
For information on the rules and order of delegations at standing committee and Council meetings, please refer to our Consolidated Procedure Bylaw (059-2024).
Give us your feedback
After speaking at a committee or Council meeting, please take a few minutes to give us your feedback  on the process of registering and delegating.

A BY-LAW TO AUTHORIZE THE IMPOSITION OF A SPECIAL CHARGE UNDER THE
BETTER HOMES LANARK PROGRAM IN ACCORDANCE WITH ONTARIO
REGULATION 586/06 FOR THE PROPERTY DESCRIBED AS 16 SARAH STREET,
CARLETON PLACE K7C 2Z5
WHEREAS Lanark County received funding from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities
and Council enacted By-Law 2025-09, a by-law to adopt a local improvement charge
residential retrofit program known as ‘Better Homes Lanark’, in accordance with Part III of
Ontario Regulation 586/06, Local Improvement Charges - Priority Lien Status, enacted under
the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25 (“O. Reg. 586/06”) and have developed the
program to be implemented in local municipalities;
AND WHEREAS the Council of the Town of Carleton Place enacted By-Law No. 11-2025, a
by-law to adopt a local improvement charge residential retrofit program known as ‘Better
Homes Lanark’, in accordance with Part III of Ontario Regulation 586/06, Local Improvement
Charges - Priority Lien Status, enacted under the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25 (“O.
Reg. 586/06”) for the municipality;
AND WHEREAS the owner(s) of the Benefitting Property, the County of Lanark and the
Town of Carleton Place, have entered into a Property Owner Agreement (the “POA”)
pursuant to Section 36.2 of O. Reg. 586/06 for the Applicant to undertake work as a local
improvement (the “Work”) on the Benefitting Property and to raise the cost of the Work (the
“Cost”) by imposing a special charge on the Benefitting Property;
AND WHEREAS the Town of Carleton Place Clerk has certified the POA pursuant to
Section 36.4 of O. Reg. 586/06;
AND WHEREAS the Work has been completed;
AND WHEREAS a local improvement roll was prepared in accordance with Section 36.10
of O. Reg. 586/06, setting out the Cost, the proposed special charges to be imposed on
the Benefitting Property, when the special charges are to be paid, and the lifetime of the
Work;
AND WHEREAS the County of Lanark has given notice of the proposed local improvement
roll to the owner(s) of the Benefitting Property pursuant to Section 36.11 of O. Reg. 586/06;
AND WHEREAS the Treasurer of the Town of Carleton Place has certified the proposed
local improvement roll in accordance with Section 36.11(2) of O. Reg. 586/06;
AND WHEREAS Section 36.14 of O. Reg. 586/06 provides that after the Treasurer has
certified the local improvement roll, the Town of Carleton Place shall by by-law provide that
the amount specially charged on the lot set out in the roll shall be sufficient to raise the lot’s
share of the cost by a number of equal annual payments and that a special charge shall be
imposed in each year on the lot equal to the amount of the payment payable in that year;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Council of the Town of Carleton Place
enacts as follows:
1 of 3
BY-LAW NO. 62-2026
GENERAL REGULATIONS:
1. The provisions of Section 36.14 of O. Reg. 586/06 apply to the Benefitting Property
as a result of the completion of the Work pursuant to the POA.
2. The amounts specially charged on the lot as set out in the certified local
improvement roll attached as Schedule “A” to this By-Law (the “Special Charge -
Actual”) is sufficient to raise the lot’s share of the Cost, along with interest, and shall
be imposed on and collected by annually adding the annual amount payable as set
out in Schedule A to this By-Law to the tax roll of the lot.
3. The Annual Payments as set out in certified local improvement roll attached as
Schedule A do not extend beyond the lifetime of the Work.
4. The amount of each payment made in respect of the Special Charge shall be
entered in the local improvement roll by the Treasurer.
ULTRA VIRES
5. Should any sections of this by-law, including any section or part of any schedules
attached hereto be declared by a court of competent jurisdiction to be ultra vires, the
remaining sections shall nevertheless remain valid and binding.
FORCE AND EFFECT
6. This By-Law shall come into force and take effect on the date of its passing and
shall be deemed repealed on the date on which the Treasurer certifies that the
Special Charge has been paid in full.

COMMUNICATION 137060
Received From: Ross Rankin, Property and Project Manager
Addressed To: Council
Date: June 25, 2026
Topic: Hot (Therapeutic) Pool Basin Failure and Other Recent Issues
SUMMARY
The purpose of this report is to request funds for the supply and installation of a new
Diamond Brite plaster surface and to complete other repairs for the hot (therapeutic)
pool at Carambeck due to failure and age of the plaster basin.
BACKGROUND
On November 5, 2025, Pool staff notified the Property Management Division that the hot
pool basin plaster floor surface had lifted in areas down to the concrete substrate. The
issue was investigated by staff and a temporary solution to keep the pool open for the
day was made.
Property Management began to investigate options to complete the repair and notified
the Manager of Recreation and Culture that the pool would be required to be shut down
for a period. Staff then notified Council by email of the shut down.
The initial repair was completed and the hot pool reopened November 15, 2025.
Unfortunately, the initial repair did not hold, and arrangements were made to shut down
the pool for an extended period to complete the proper repair. The pool was again shut
down on November 24, 2025 where the initial failed areas were repaired along with
other areas that had lifted. Council was notified by staff of the shutdown. The repairs
were completed and the pool reopened on December 12, 2025.
On April 1, 2026, Property Management was informed that more areas of the plaster
basin had delaminated, and the floor was becoming rough. There are concerns that the
plaster surface would continue to fail. Staff contacted the original vendor (Benson pools)
that supplied and installed the Diamond Brite plaster in 2015 for them to complete an
assessment. The vendor indicated that they were unable to meet until April 28, 2026 –
this was deemed by staff to be an unacceptable wait to address the situation. Another
commercial pool vendor, from Ottawa, GBI Pools, was contacted for an assessment,
and a site meeting was held on April 15, 2026. GBI Pools indicated that the product life
expectancy is 10 years; the surface is now 11 years old – past its expected lifecycle
date.
GBI Pools have provided an option to repair the basin with no warranty as it may
continue to fail and an option to replace the basin by removing the Diamond Brite
plaster down to the concrete substrate and install a new Diamond Brite plaster surface
that will last for approximately 10 years.
Staff met onsite with Benson Pools on April 28, 2026 to have them complete the
assessment. They recommended that the basin not be repaired and recommended that
it be replaced with the same process and product as identified by GBI Pools.
Both GBI Pools and Benson Pools provided quotes for the replacement.
COMMENTS
The Recreation and Culture Division has identified time in August that could be made
available to complete the repair or replacement of the Diamond Brite plaster.
The quotes obtained were as follows:

Three (3) additional failures have occurred at Carambeck in the last two (2) weeks and
need to be addressed:
 Last week, the hot pool filtration system had one (1) of the two (2) tanks fail. The
replacement is currently being sourced, and the expected cost is approximately
$5,000.00.
 The controls system for the 25m pool that operates the dehumidification and
heating of the pool water has failed. Currently the water is being heated, and the
air is not being dehumidified. Our vendor that maintains this for us is sourcing out
a temporary fix. This would allow for the air to be dehumidified, and the pool
water will not be heated. The water will have to be heated by the natural gas
boilers instead of using free heating from the dehumidification process.
 The PAL2 Aquatic lift is out of service. The wheels require replacement. AMB Lift
is sourcing the wheel replacement. This is an accessible lift to assist people into
the pool.
Staff are getting estimates for these recent failures, however, based on previous similar
works, ballpark estimates indicate these repairs could total $24,000.
This is being brought forward to the Committee of the Whole to decide on to what level
of investment is acceptable by Council for the current pool facility. A companion report
to this report, also presented at the Special meeting on June 25, 2026, discusses further
investment in the Carambeck pool facility in detail.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
The total unfunded budgeted amount for these works is a minimum of $50,697.48 plus
HST. As HST is added to the costs for use of the facility, the Town receives a full HST
rebate. As a result, the net price to the Town is $50,697.48.
Obtaining final estimates for the filter, control system and lift are still in progress. The
ballpark estimate to address all immediate needs for the pool is approximately $75,000.
Council could consider another recommendation regarding these three (3) additional
items at the Special Meeting on June 25, 2026 once pricing has been obtained.

COMMUNICATION 137059

Topic Procurement Strategy for New Recreation Facility
SUMMARY
Following discussion of the New Recreation Facility report, Staff are presenting options
for the procurement strategy of the pool project. A design-build procurement strategy is
recommended for its efficiencies with respect to schedule and overall project cost.
BACKGROUND
The Town’s Strategic Plan 2023-2026 included the priority to develop a “Multi-Use
Recreation Facility Concept Plan”. The Parks, Recreation and Culture Master Plan
(PRCMP) priority 53 discussed that current needs with respect to an aquatic facility, are
being met based on the current population. Priority 53 then recommends an additional
pool to meet the needs of a growing community but not until 2038. Priority 55 of the
PRCMP recommends a new recreation facility south of Highway 7 that would include
meeting rooms and a gymnasium at a minimum which also speaks to the need for a
facility of this type.
Staff began to prepare an overall schedule to move forward with the project design.
Summary timeline:
 On March 11, 2025 – Council gave approval to staff to develop a plan to replace
the Town’s aging indoor pool.
 A session in June 2025 led by +VG Architects presented conceptual designs for
an addition onto the Carleton Place Arena. The scope for this included an
elevated walking track, pool, gymnasium and auditorium. Staff returned to
Council in June 2025 to present these conceptual designs for information.
 In January 2026, staff presented a business plan to assess the feasibility of a
steel-walled pool system within a Sprung structure for consideration. At this
meeting, council emphasized community consultation.
 In April 21, 2026, staff returned to Council with a report on the Recreation
Concept Plan and next steps. Council decided to not move forward with public
consultation and directed staff to consult the Working Group on next steps.
 The Recreation Concept Plan Working Group met on May 28, 2026 to discuss
options for next steps on the new recreation facility. One of the outcomes of this
meeting was to develop the procurement strategy for the new facility to Council at
a special meeting in June. This report addresses this direction.
A detailed project timeline can be found in the New Recreation Facility Way Forward
report
DISCUSSION
The options are as follows:
 Non-competitive process
 Traditional Design-Bid-Build process
 Design-Build process
Staff are aware of other options for the procurement of such a facility however, only the
relevant strategies for this context are discussed in this report.
Non-Competitive Procurements
A non-competitive procurement approach has been identified as a potential option for
Council’s consideration, based on the availability of a qualified proponent with
demonstrated experience in delivering comparable aquatic and recreation facilities.
This option has been previously presented to Committee of the Whole to provide
context on alternative delivery methods.
While a non-competitive approach can offer benefits such as reduced procurement
timelines and access to specialized expertise, without the benefit of competitive bidding,
the municipality may be perceived as having limited its ability to test market pricing,
innovation, and quality benchmarks. This may raise concerns about the project with
respect to transparency, fairness, and value for taxpayers.
A key disadvantage of a non-competitive procurement approach is the heightened
reputational and governance risk to the municipality if the project is not delivered to the
expected quality, performance, or value standards. Additionally, schedule or budget
slippages will face additional scrutiny under this approach. Resident confidence in
Council’s decision‑making may also be adversely impacted.
Additionally, the Town may face increased project criticism from residents, the media,
and oversight bodies (i.e. funders). These reputational risks are amplified for complex,
high‑profile recreation facility projects such as this. Service expectations are high
among residents; this project has already gained significant traction and interest with
community members. Project outcomes are highly visible, underscoring the importance
of a competitive process and robust justification if a non‑competitive procurement
method is to be considered.
Staff are not recommending this approach as it does not meet the parameters within the
Town’s Procurement By-law for non-competitive procurement and are presenting this
option for information purposes only.
Traditional Design-Bid-Build Process
Staff would retain a consultant team to fully design the facility. The project would then be
tendered, and construction would be awarded to the lowest bidder who meets the
requirements of the procurement document.
Under the traditional design‑bid‑build procurement strategy, the municipality retains a
consulting team to complete the full design of the aquatic facility, including pool
systems, mechanical and electrical infrastructure, structural elements, and gymnasium
spaces, prior to tendering construction.
Once detailed drawings and specifications are complete, the project is competitively
tendered, and a separate construction contract is awarded to the lowest compliant
bidder, consistent with Ontario municipal procurement requirements for transparency,
fairness, and open competition.
This approach provides the municipality with a high level of control over the design and
allows Council, staff, and stakeholders to review and approve detailed plans for
specialized spaces such as pools, change rooms, and gymnasium areas before
construction pricing is established.

WHEREAS The Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, authorizes the Council of every municipality
to pass by-laws for governing the proceedings of its Council, the conduct of its members
and the calling of meetings; and
WHEREAS Section 238 (2) further indicates that every municipality and local board shall
pass a procedure by-law for governing the calling, place and proceedings of meetings;
WHEREAS The Council shall also follow the regulations as set out within the Municipal
Conflict of Interest Act; and the parliamentary authority of Roberts Rules of Order;
AND WHEREAS following report GR-030-2019, the Council of the Municipality of
Casselman deems it advisable to amend By-Law No. 2019-026 as hereinafter set forth;
NOW THEREFORE the Council of the Municipality of Casselman enacts as follows:
1. That the following provision of sections of By-law No. 2019-026 are hereby amended
and reads as follows:
Section 4.1 Inaugural – time – place - held:
“The Inaugural Meeting of the Council, following a regular election, shall be
considered the Councils First meeting and shall be held on the First Tuesday in
December, of an election year, beginning at 6:00 p.m. in accordance to the
Municipal Elections Act Sec.16. ”
Section 4.2 Regular – Schedule – designated - time:
“The next and each succeeding regular meeting shall be held on the second and
fourth Tuesdays of each month, commencing at 6:00 p.m. At such place within
the Municipality of Casselman designated for such purpose by the Council and
shall be held in accordance with the schedule of meetings of Council and the
Committees of Council prepared by the Clerk.”
Section 4.2.1 Alteration of the date of a Council meeting:
“Council may alter the date and/or time of a Council meeting provided that a notice
of 48 hours (calculated on open days) is posted on the municipal Web site. A
Council meeting may also be canceled within 24 hours in case of an
emergency.”
Section 4.4 Exception to meetings:
“Notwithstanding the provisions of Section 4.2 and 4.3 of this By-law, there shall
be: one meeting of Council in the month of February, which shall be held on the
second Tuesday of the month; no meetings during the March break, one
meeting of Council in the month of July, which shall be held on the second Tuesday
of the month; one meeting of Council in the month of August, which shall be held
on the fourth Tuesday of the month and one meeting of Council in the month of
December, which shall be held on the second Tuesday of the month. Should the
meeting fall on a public or civic holiday, the Council shall meet at the same hour
on the next following day, which is not a public or civic holiday.”
Section 4.11 In Camera Meeting – closed to public - Time:
“In Camera meetings, shall commence at a time prescribed by the City Clerk
and/or Chief Administrative Officer upon consultation with the Mayor and the
meetings shall be adjourned no later than 5:55 p.m. if occurring before the
public meeting”. An in camera meeting can also occur after the public
meeting”.
Section 33.6 Meeting – continuation – 9:00 p.m.:
“No item of business other than the Confirmatory By-law shall be considered at a
meeting of the Council after the hour of 9:00 p.m. local time, unless otherwise
decided by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Members present. The duration of a
Council meeting shall not exceed a total of 3 hours (including in camera
meeting), unless otherwise decided by a two-thirds (2/3) vote a of the
Members present.”
Section 21.13 Committee meetings:
“No meeting shall be scheduled between the second Tuesday of the month
of July and the 4th Tuesday of August.”
2. That all other provisions of By-law No. 2019-026 will continue to be in force.
3. That this by-law shall come into effect on the passing thereof.

Council Meetings
Regular Council Meetings are held on the First and Third Monday of every month at 5:00 PM, unless otherwise stated on our 2026 Council Meeting Calendar. Visit the Council Portal to view Agendas, Minutes, and Committee Meetings.
If you wish to address Council at a Council Meeting, please submit a deputation request prior to 12:00 PM (noon) the Wednesday prior to the meeting.
If you wish to submit a proclamation request, please refer to By-law 41-2025 and complete the online proclamation request form. 
Closed Council Meetings
Municipal councils, local boards, and their committees must meet behind closed doors on occasion to deal with some matters. The purpose of a closed meeting is to receive information or give direction. Local government in Ontario must be transparent and accountable. To this end, the Province has set the rules for a council, local board, or a committee to go into a closed meeting. These rules are found in section 239 of the Municipal Act 2001 and they must be strictly followed.

Types of Council Meetings
SECTION MENU
Cobourg Municipal Council conducts its business through Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Standing Committee Meetings
Standing Committees are affiliated with municipal divisions and overall priorities and policy decisions. Cobourg will now have three Standing Committees consisting of:
Community Services, Protection and Economic Development Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 9:30 a.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Adam Bureau (Chair), Councillor Aaron Burchat, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Public Works, Development Division Standing Committee
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Brian Darling (Chair), Councillor Miriam Mutton, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Corporate, Finance, and Legislative Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Thursday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Deputy Mayor Nicole Beatty (Chair), Councillor Randy Barber, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Other Members of Council can attend standing committees of which they are not members to ask questions and hear information to prepare for Regular Council Meetings. Standing Committee members discuss items on the agenda and make a recommendation to Council for the action to be taken on the matter.
Regular Council Meetings
Following the Standing Committee meetings the recommendations of the Committees will be presented at a Regular Council meeting where a final decision will be made and published in the meeting minutes. See the calendar below for meeting information including dates and times, and to access Agendas, Minutes, and videos. Unless otherwise noted, meetings are open to the general public. 
Other Types of Council Meetings
The following meeting types are held by the Town of Cobourg Council:
Standing Committee
Regular Council
Public Council
Special Council
Emergency Council
Advisory Committees and Local Boards, and
Closed Council
The public may attend any of these meetings, except Closed Council meetings. Closed meetings are held in accordance with section 239 of the Municipal Act, 2001. 
See above for information on Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Public Meetings
Public Council meetings are held to provide an opportunity for Council to receive comments from the public to assist Council in making a final decision. Public meetings are generally held on the third Wednesday of the month at 5 p.m.
Public meetings are held when changes to the following are being considered:
Certain by-laws (ie. Zoning By-law);
Licensing and Fees;
Master Plans (Parks, Waterfront, Parking, Transportation);
Official Plans; and
Other matters requiring public input.
Closed Meeting Investigator
Any person can request an investigation to see if Council has met in Closed Session for a valid, legal reason.
The Town of Cobourg has an Integrity Commissioner, Closed Meeting Investigator and Ombudsman. Fill in the Request Form for Closed Meeting Investigation and send it to the Legislative Services Department with the $25 fee.

Expression of Interest Update to ERO 026-419 Municipal Service Corporation, Deputy Mayor Fryer
  Recommendation:
WHEREAS Collingwood’s Community Based Strategic Plan is based on “Working together to provide excellent services, progressive and accountable decision-making, collaboration and advocacy”, and
WHEREAS both AMO and ROMA have stated that they believe a Municipal Services Corporation(MSC) model is a valid and potentially helpful governance and organizational tool for some municipalities to take advantage of, and
WHEREAS on Aug. 10/26 Council reconsidered and determined that an Expression of Interest be submitted, for ERO Notice 026-419 regarding a Water and Waste Water Public Corporation Model (PSC) prior to an Aug 13/26 deadline, and
WHEREAS Ontario announced on Aug. 15/26 that ERO 026-419 would remain open for 120 days(Dec. 11/26) to provide municipalities sufficient time to submit an EOI and further advised that future extensions may be implemented, and
WHEREAS the Town of Collingwood Long Term Strategic Financial Plan is imminent in completion to assist with consideration of models for delivering among other things, water and wastewater services, and
WHEREAS Collingwood has a rich history of separated governance, with the former Collingwood Public Utilities Commission/Service Board, that provided effective and efficient recommendations on municipal potable and non-potable water service operations to Council dating back to 1889 through to 2015 when Council dissolved the structure and invoked their sole governance of all municipal water service operational responsibilities, and
WHEREAS Council had unanimously directed for only continued advocacy when receiving Staff Report CAO2026-05 titled MSCs, which provided general information regarding a possible restoration of separated governance to assist Council in decision making on water and wastewater through the Municipal Act, 2001 (Ontario Regulation 599/06) that currently allows for the formation of a MSC, and
WHEREAS CAO 2026-05 recommended not to proceed any further, at the time, with regards to separate governance steps but Council has now indicated that a consideration of possible alternative models should be undertaken, and
WHEREAS the initial pilot of a new PSC for the Region of Peel will not take effect until 2029, but an MSC could be established and operational much earlier, thereby if required providing a working model for comparison in the future to the Peel model of water and wastewater governance and operations,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council hereby directs that an update CAO Staff Report that include the EOI plan submitted for Aug. 13/26 and any pertinent further details about establishing a MSC, as well as an overview of Innisfil’s governance structure, reporting to Council and the overall operational structure for their MSC Innservices(established in 2015 to independently oversee water and wastewater financing, building and operation), and
THAT Council requires that the update be provided at the next regular meeting of Council and Committee of the Whole for further consideration of next steps, which may include additional submission details for the EOI plan that has already been submitted for ERO 026-419 for Aug. 13/26.

SECTION MENU
Regular Open Council meetings commence at 7:00 p.m. on the second and fourth Mondays of the month. These meetings are open to the public. Planning and Special meetings are scheduled as required and public notice is provided per the legislation.
Closed Council meetings commence at 6:00 p.m., prior to the open sessions at 7:00 p.m.  Closed sessions are not open to the public in accordance with Section 239 of the Municipal Act. 
Agendas and Minutes
Agendas and Minutes of Open Council meetings will be published on the City's website on the Friday before the regularly scheduled meetings. This includes agendas and minutes for Open Council, Special, and Public meetings, as well as meetings of City of Dryden boards and committees.

To watch City of Dryden Council and OPP Detachment Board meetings live, please access the Council and OPP Detachment Board Meeting Calendar and open the agenda for the meeting you wish to watch.  The video will stream live on the agenda page in the top left corner or cursor down on the calendar to view the table and click on the video icon for the meeting you wish to watch. Following the live stream of the meeting, the video icon will disappear. Once the video has been time stamped, it will be posted again for viewing by the public usually within a day of the meeting.
