Delegations
When a member of the community wants to speak to Council during an Open Meeting, it is called a delegation. In order to do this, you must fill out a delegation request. This can be done online here, or you can complete a hard copy at the Clerk's Office located at 30 Van Horne Avenue. 
  Closed Meeting Investigator
Municipal Councils must conduct business only at meetings that are open to the public but there are some exceptions where we have closed meetings. Members of the public have the right to submit a complaint if they feel the Municipality held a closed meeting that did not follow the rules/exemptions listed in the Municipal Act, 2001, Section 239.2 (1).
The Closed Meeting Investigator's role is to conduct investigations upon receipt of a complaint in respect of meetings or part of meetings that are closed to the public to determine compliance with the Act or the Municipality's Procedural By-law and to report the results of such investigations to Council.
Our Municipality has appointed Ombudsman Ontario to investigate any complaints made to them by the public about closed meetings. 
Their duties include:
Conducting an investigation when they receive a complaint about a meeting or part of a meeting that is closed to the public
Determining whether the meeting complied with the Municipal Act and Municipal Procedural By-law
Reporting the results of the investigation

TOWNSHIP OF EDWARDSBURGH CARDINAL
INFORMATION ITEM
Committee: Committee of the Whole – Administration and Operations
Date: September 14, 2026
Department: Fire
Topic: 2026 Interim MTO Report
Background: When the Fire Department responds to an emergency on a provincially
owned highway and performs eligible services, the Ministry of Transportation (MTO)
reimburses the Municipality at a rate of $583.05 per vehicle per hour, for up to three
vehicles, unless extenuating circumstances require additional apparatus.
To qualify for reimbursement, all services performed, supplies used, and the purpose of
each responding fire apparatus must be thoroughly documented. Only apparatus that
performs MTO-approved services are eligible for payment. Where multiple fire
departments respond to the same incident, only one claim may be submitted to the
MTO. Once payment is received, the host municipality distributes the reimbursement to
the participating municipalities as appropriate.
Eligible services include:
 Vehicle extrication/stabilization
 Fire extinguishment
 Traffic control
 Spill cleanup
 Hazmat
 Standby if Requested by OPP
Responses that do not require an approved service are not eligible for reimbursement.
Examples include rendering first aid only, vehicles in the ditch where no approved
service is provided, false alarms, or instances when an incident is not found.
Reducing the number of non-billable MTO responses has been identified as a priority by
the Ontario Association of Fire Chiefs (OAFC). In response, the Fire Department
continues to carefully document all highway incidents and submit claims only when
eligible services have been provided. This approach significantly reduces administrative
time associated with preparing and tracking ineligible invoices while also minimizing
unnecessary exposure of personnel who would otherwise be required to collect
information on active highways solely for billing purposes.
Page 1 of 2
Fire Department officers continue to demonstrate sound operational judgment by
assigning personnel to perform MTO-approved services that are appropriate to the
incident. This ensures public and firefighter safety while maximizing the Municipality's
ability to recover eligible response costs.

Topic: OPP Grenville Detachment – 2025 Annual Board Report
Purpose: To present to Council the 2025 OPP Detachment Board Annual Report
Background: Ontario’s Community Safety and Policing Act (CSPA) came into effect on
April 1, 2024, replacing the Police Services Act and introducing reforms intended to
modernize policing and improve community safety.
A key change was the creation of OPP Detachment Boards for each Ontario Provincial
Police detachment. The South Grenville OPP Detachment Board serves the Township
of Edwardsburgh Cardinal, Township of Augusta, and Town of Prescott and consists of
eight members:
3 municipal council representatives
3 community representatives
2 provincial representatives
The Board’s responsibilities include setting policing objectives and priorities, advising
and monitoring the Detachment Commander, participating in the selection of the
Commander, reviewing policing reports, and providing an annual report to the
municipalities by June 30 each year.
The report is being brought directly to the three municipal Councils to meet the CSPA’s
annual reporting requirement, rather than waiting for the next South Grenville OPP
Detachment Board meeting scheduled for September 10, 2026.
The report is intended to ensure the South Grenville OPP Detachment Board complies
with its new statutory annual reporting obligation and keeps the three municipalities
informed about policing services provided in their communities.
Policy Implications: None
Strategic Plan Implications: None

municipalities included in the South Grenville Detachment Board and is included in the
2026 budget.

Topic: 2026 Drinking Water Quality Management Standard (DWQMS) Re-accreditation
Audit Results
Purpose: To provide Council with the results from the Townships 2026 DWQMS
re-accreditation audit.
Background:
Under the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), all municipal residential drinking water
system operating authorities are required to maintain accreditation to the DWQMS. As
part of this legislative requirement, operating authorities undergo an external re-
accreditation audit every three years to verify continued conformance with the DWQMS.
In preparation for the re-accreditation audit, a desktop audit review was completed by
NSF International on June 4th. The audit identified three minor Corrective Action
Requests (CARs) related to procedural documentation within the Township's Quality
Management System. Environmental Services staff reviewed the findings, updated the
applicable procedures, and submitted corrective actions to the auditor. All corrective
actions were subsequently reviewed and approved.
The subsequent on-site re-accreditation audit on July 9th confirmed that all previous
corrective actions had been effectively addressed and recommended continued
accreditation of the Township's Drinking Water Quality Management System. The audit
resulted in no non-conformances and identified six Opportunities for Improvement
(OFIs). These OFIs are recommendations to further improve the Township's Quality
Management System and do not affect the Township's accreditation status. Staff will
incorporate the recommendations into the Township's continual improvement process.
Page 1 of 2
Policy Implications:
The Township's Drinking Water Quality Management System remains compliant with
the requirements of the Safe Drinking Water Act, and conformance to the Drinking
Water Quality Management Standard (DWQMS). Maintaining accreditation is a
legislative requirement for municipal residential drinking water system operating
authorities in Ontario.
Strategic Plan Implications:
Maintaining accreditation under the Drinking Water Quality Management Standard
supports Council's strategic objective of providing safe, reliable, and sustainable
municipal infrastructure and services while demonstrating a commitment to continual
improvement and regulatory compliance.
Financial Considerations:
There are no direct financial implications associated with receiving this report.

Application
The applicant is seeking relief from Zoning By-law 07-67, as amended, to permit a
proposed accessory building (detached garage). A Minor Variance application has been
submitted, requesting the following relief:
 Section 4.2.2.2 – Location: To permit an accessory building to be constructed in
front of the front building line of the main building, whereas all accessory buildings
shall be constructed to the rear of the front building line of the main building.
Section 4.2.3 – Building Height: To permit an accessory building with a maximum
building height of 7.0 m, whereas the maximum building height for an accessory
building shall not exceed 4.5 m.
A location map, site plan, floor plan and elevations illustrating the proposal are included
in this report as Attachments A, B and C.
Recommendation
It is the opinion of Planning Staff that the variances are minor in nature, desirable for the
appropriate development of the land, and meet the intent of the Town of Erin’s Official
Plan and Zoning By-law and therefore recommend Approval.

The subject property is designated Country Residential in the Town of Erin’s Official Plan
and zoned Rural Residential (R3-103) in the Town’s Zoning By-law 07-67, as amended.
The property is also located in the Protected Countryside of the Greenbelt Plan and
identified as part of the Natural Heritage System.
The subject property is approximately 0.8 ha. (2 acres) in area with a frontage of 59.62 m
(195.6 ft) along Erinwood Drive. The property currently contains an existing single
detached dwelling and shed. The Applicant is proposing to construct an accessory
building consisting of a garage with a second storey for storage purposes.

Re: Support Resolution Regarding a Feasibility Study for Highway 407
Please be advised that the Council of The Corporation of the Town of Orangeville, at its
Regular Council Meeting held on February 10, 2025, approved the following resolution:
Whereas road safety has been identified as a priority for Town of
Orangeville Council, staff, and residents; and
Whereas significant increases in truck traffic on Highway 10 have led to
safety concerns along the entire corridor from Melancthon down to the
southern point of Caledon; and
Whereas trucking companies avoid Highway 407 due to its tolls, leading
to higher volumes of traffic on other roads and highways; and
Whereas a pilot project to subsidize truck lanes on Highway 407 would
provide valuable insights into the economic and road safety impact of
diverting truck traffic to the 407; and
Therefore be it resolved that the Town of Orangeville support the City of
Vaughan's recent resolution to request that the Province of Ontario
implement a one-year pilot program that will subsidize or eliminate tolls
for dedicated truck lanes on Highway 407, evaluating the impact on
overall transportation efficiency and road safety; and
Be it further resolved that a copy of this motion be circulated to Premier
Doug Ford, Hon. Sylvia Jones, Deputy Premier and Dufferin-Caledon
MPP, Hon. Prabmeet Sarkaria, Minister of Transportation, Steven Del
Duca, Mayor of the City of Vaughan and all Dufferin municipalities.
Carried Unanimously

Public Participation at Town of Gravenhurst Meetings
POLICY STATEMENT:
It is the policy of the Corporation of the Town of Gravenhurst to permit electronic participation from
members of the public during Council, Boards and SubCommittee meetings.
PURPOSE
To provide processes and a framework for electronic participation at meetings.
APPLICATION
This Policy applies to all members of the public who chose to participate in a meeting electronically.
PROCEDURE & GUIDELINES
A. General
The Town of Gravenhurst uses the MVI EasyConf Connect Conference system to facilitate electronic
audio-visual participation in Council and Committee meetings. Members of the public who have
access to a reliable internet connection, a camera and microphone may participate in a meeting
electronically versus exclusively in-person.
Members of the public wishing to participate electronically are encouraged to download the EasyConf
Connect application on their computers or smart devices. Web browsers can be used; however,
functionality may differ.
Electronic participants will receive an email before the meeting with a private link to access the
meeting. Depending on the meeting type, the participant may remain within a waiting room until their
item is on the agenda. All are encouraged to follow along through the livestream on the Town’s
YouTube channel. Note that the livestream may be 15 to 30 seconds delayed depending on the
connection.
B. Connectivity
Members of the public participating in a meeting electronically are responsible for ensuring the
reliability of their connection for the duration of their allotted time at the meeting. If a participant loses
connectivity during the meeting for more than 2 consecutive minutes, they will be deemed to have left
the meeting.
Technical support is not available during a live meeting.
While electronic participation is available for the public, the meeting’s primary location is in-person
inside the Council Chambers. The meeting will continue regardless of the participant’s ability to
connect or maintain a connection electronically.
C. Deputations
Deputations are presentations of up to 10 minutes made at Committee of the Whole, Planning
Council or Subcommittee meetings from an individual or group of persons. Additional information
regarding deputations is included within the Procedural By-law.
Deputation requests are required to be submitted in writing through the online deputation request
form. Deputations may be permitted in-person in the Council Chambers or electronically.
Those requesting an electronic deputation may do so by selecting electronic participation on their
form. Multiple accounts are permitted for deputations and must be clearly identified including
complete email addresses.
Visual presentations (PowerPoint, pdf, video etc.) are permitted during deputations. Those presenting
in-person shall submit the materials by noon the day prior to the meeting allowing the materials to be
pre-loaded into the audio-visual system. Electronic participants will be able to share their screens
directly within the audio-visual system. Please note, however, that screen sharing is not supported on
mobile devices. If your deputation includes a visual presentation, you will need to connect via a
computer.
Presentations not provided in advance may be displayed if the participant brings their own laptop with
a HDMI port.
Phones and tablets are not compatible with the audio-visual equipment.
D. Public Meetings
Public Meetings are public hearings hosted in accordance with the Planning Act to obtain public input
on Development Services matters. They generally occur during Planning Council and Committee of
Adjustment meetings.

  8.1
Review of Service Equity, Community Engagement and Municipal Investment Across Greater Sudbury
  As presented by Councillor Parent:

WHEREAS the City of Greater Sudbury is comprised of many distinct communities with unique histories, identities, and service needs;

AND WHEREAS residents across Greater Sudbury have expressed interest in ensuring that municipal services, infrastructure investments, and engagement opportunities are delivered in a fair, transparent, and equitable manner throughout the municipality;

AND WHEREAS Council recognizes the importance of fostering strong community connections, supporting local identity, and ensuring that all residents feel represented and informed in municipal decision-making;

AND WHEREAS Council wishes to better understand whether opportunities exist to improve transparency regarding municipal investments, strengthen community engagement, and enhance service delivery across all areas of the municipality;

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Greater Sudbury directs that staff undertake a review and prepare a report examining opportunities to strengthen service equity, community engagement, and transparency of municipal investment throughout the City of Greater Sudbury, including:
A review of municipal practices used in comparable Ontario and Canadian municipalities to support equitable service delivery, local engagement, and transparent capital investment planning;
The feasibility of developing area-based reporting, investment tracking, or other mechanisms that provide residents and Council with greater transparency regarding infrastructure and capital investments across the municipality;
Opportunities to enhance resident engagement and communication regarding municipal programs, services, and long-term planning initiatives.
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that staff engage residents, community organizations, business groups, and other relevant stakeholders as part of the review process;

AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that staff report back to Council with findings and recommendations no later than the end of the second quarter of 2027.
8.2
Short-Term Rentals Restricting Occupancy
  As presented by Councillor McIntosh:

WHEREAS City Council for the City of Greater Sudbury approved amendments to the Zoning By-law and the Registration of Certain Businesses By-law in 2024 to permit and regulate short-term rental accommodations; 

AND WHEREAS since the implementation of these amendments, the City of Greater Sudbury has experienced an increase in the number of short-term rentals operating within larger residential dwellings; 

AND WHEREAS larger dwellings may accommodate higher numbers of guests, which can result in impacts on surrounding neighbourhoods, including excessive noise, increased traffic and parking pressures, non-compliance with property standards, and disregard for regulations such as open-air burning and fire restrictions; 

AND WHEREAS some short-term rental properties are located in areas serviced by private septic systems, which may be subject to increased strain from higher occupancy levels, potentially posing risks to nearby water bodies and drinking water sources; 

AND WHEREAS several municipalities in Ontario have adopted short-term rental regulations that establish specific operational standards, including limits on guest occupancy and the number of bedrooms that may be rented; 

AND WHEREAS establishing reasonable occupancy limits for short-term rentals would help protect neighbourhood character, promote public safety, and support the long-term sustainability of private servicing systems;

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that the City of Greater Sudbury direct staff to prepare and present the necessary by-law amendments for Council's consideration, before the end of the first quarter of 2027, to establish occupancy limits for short-term rental accommodations at a maximum of two (2) persons per guest room, to a maximum occupancy of eight (8) persons per dwelling.
8.3
Addressing Rat Infestations in Minnow Lake and Developing a Community-Wide Rat Management Strategy
  As presented by Mayor Lefebvre:

WHEREAS residents and businesses in the Minnow Lake area have reported increased rat activity, resulting in concerns related to public health, property damage, neighbourhood livability, and quality of life;

AND WHEREAS timely action is required to assist affected residents and businesses and to address conditions that may be contributing to rat infestations within the community;

AND WHEREAS municipalities across Ontario have implemented education, prevention, monitoring, and integrated pest management initiatives to address rat infestations and reduce their impacts;

AND WHEREAS understanding the sources and contributing factors associated with rat infestations is necessary to develop effective and sustainable mitigation measures;

THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED that Council direct the Chief Administrative Officer to immediately coordinate the appropriate City departments and, where appropriate, work with community partners, Public Health Sudbury & Districts, local businesses, property owners, waste management providers, and other relevant stakeholders to take any steps deemed necessary to assist the Minnow Lake community in responding to the current rat infestation and mitigating contributing factors;

AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that such immediate actions may include enhanced inspection, monitoring, public education, community outreach, waste and litter management measures, review of municipal infrastructure and public lands, and any other appropriate measures to reduce rat harbourage and food sources in the affected area;

AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Chief Administrative Officer report back to Council with recommendations for a Rat Management and Mitigation Strategy that, while informed by the circumstances in Minnow Lake, can be applied to other areas of Greater Sudbury should similar issues arise, including:
An assessment of rat activity and contributing factors within Minnow Lake, including available data regarding reported sightings, complaints, and infestation trends;
Identification of potential sources and conditions contributing to rat activity, including waste management practices, construction activities, vacant properties, municipal infrastructure, and other harbourage conditions;
A review of best practices, policies, and programs implemented by comparable Ontario municipalities;
Recommendations for public education and awareness initiatives to assist residents, businesses, landlords, and property owners in preventing and responding to rat infestations;
Recommendations for an Integrated Pest Management approach focused on prevention, monitoring, environmental controls, and targeted mitigation measures;
Options for enhanced reporting, monitoring, and data collection to support ongoing management of rat infestations across Greater Sudbury;
Opportunities for targeted pilot programs, partnerships, or support measures for communities experiencing significant infestations;
Budget implications, resource requirements, funding opportunities, and implementation timelines associated with any recommendations;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that staff take immediate action, where feasible, to address this issue in Minnow Lake and report back to Council with findings and recommendations on a broader strategy no later than the second quarter of 2027.

General
1. Application and Interpretation
1.1. This By-law establishes the rules of order for meetings of Council and
Committee of the Whole.
1.2. A word in this By-law expressed in the singular has a corresponding meaning
when used in the plural.
1.3. Any future amendment(s) to the Municipal Act, 2001 or other legislation as
noted in this By-law may alter the provisions of the legislation referenced but
shall not affect the validity of this By-law or any part thereof.
1.4. In an event of conflict between this By-law and any superior legislation, the
provisions of the superior legislation prevail.
1.5. A specific statement or rule in this By-law has greater authority than a general
statement or rule.
1.6. Any reference to a provision of this By-law may be referred to as “Section”
notwithstanding that it may be a section, subsection, clause, or paragraph.
1.7. If there is a conflict between two or more rules in this By-law, or if there is no
specific rule on a matter, the Chair will rule and, in making a ruling, the Chair
may consult the Clerk, rely on previous rulings and practices, or refer to
Robert’s Rules of Order.
1.8. Any use of the male or female pronouns in this By-law, shall have no
significance in the interpretation and application of the terms, provisions, and
conditions of this By-law, such use is solely for the sake of convenience.
2. Principles of this By-law
The principles of parliamentary law governing Meetings includes:
2.1. The majority of Members have the right to decide.
2.2. The minority of Members have the right to be heard.
2.3. All Members have the right to information to help make decisions, unless
otherwise prevented by law.
2.4. All Members have the right to an efficient meeting.

2
2.5. All Members, Municipal Staff, and participants have the right to be treated
with respect and courtesy.
2.6. All Members have equal rights, privileges, and obligations.
3. Suspension of Rules
3.1 Rules of order provided for in this By-law may be suspended by a Two-Thirds
vote of the members of Council present and voting, with the exception of the
following circumstances:
a) Where required by law;
b) In any contract or agreement binding the Municipality;
c) Amending this By-law;
d) Requirements of Quorum.
3.2 A Motion to suspend the Rules of Procedure required by this Procedure By-
law shall not be debatable or amendable. In addition, the motion to suspend
the rules should identify the reasons that the rules are being set aside.
4. Administrative Authority of the Clerk
4.1 The Clerk is authorized to revise or correct by-laws, minutes, and other
records or documents relating to Council and Committee for technical,
typographical, or other administrative errors and omissions for the purpose of
ensuring an accurate and complete record of proceedings and general
housekeeping.

From: Vicki McDonald, Manager of Legislative Services/Clerk

Report: CL-10-26
Subject Declaration of Council Vacancy
Recommendation
That Report CL-10-26 Declaration of Council Vacancy be received; and
That council declare the office of Councillor Harold Fleet vacant, in accordance with
section 259 of the Municipal Act, 2001; and
That council direct the office remain vacant for the remainder of the current term of council
which concludes November 15, 2026.
Background
Vacancies on municipal council are governed by sections 259 to 263 of the Municipal Act,
2001 (the Act). The Act requires that council declare a seat vacant at one of its next two
meetings when a vacancy occurs as a result of the death of a member of council.
The Act also stipulates that should the vacancy occur 90 days before voting day in a
regular election, the municipality is not required to fill the vacancy. The next regular
municipal and school board election is scheduled to take place Monday October 26, 2026
with the new four year term of office commencing November 16, 2026.
Discussion
Following the passing of Councillor Harold Fleet, the office to which he was elected
became vacant pursuant to the Act. Accordingly, council is required to formally declare
the office vacant. As the vacancy occurred near the end of the current term of council and
the next regular municipal election is scheduled for October 26, 2026, council may leave
the seat vacant for the remainder of the term, subject to the applicable provisions of the
Act.
Consequently quorum will be calculated as a majority of the members of council
excluding the vacant office. As council consists of seven members and one seat is
vacant, quorum will remain at four members for the balance of the current term.
The new term of council will commence on November 16, 2026, at which time the
members elected in the 2026 municipal election will be sworn into office.

Staff Report To Council
From: Andrew Wilken, Director of Development & Infrastructure / CBO and Sherri
Walden, CAO

Report: PB-18-26
Subject Grey County Hybrid Planning Services Model Direction
Recommendation
That Report PB-18-26 Grey County Hybrid Planning Services Model Direction be
received; and
That council opt out of the Grey County Hybrid Planning Services Model at this time; and
That the Town of Hanover communicates council’s decision to Grey County staff.
Background
A. Grey County Hybrid Planning Services Model Background
On August 8, 2024, council members attended a special Grey County joint council
meeting involving all 9 municipal councils. At this meeting, County staff provided an
overview of the proposed centralized planning service delivery model. Further to this
meeting and information, input was provided to the County with respect to council and
staff questions, clarifications and feedback.
At the March 21, 2025, joint councils meeting, County staff presented Report PDR-SJM-
19-25 Hybrid Planning Services Model Update with 4 members of Hanover Council in
attendance at this joint meeting. The direction from this meeting was that correspondence
be sent to each member municipality in Grey County, requesting any interested
municipality to indicate its support in-principle for a hybrid planning service delivery model
no later than May 9, 2025.
At the April 22, 2025, meeting, council received Report CAO-10-25 Grey County Hybrid
Planning Services Delivery Model (attached) and approved the following resolution:
That Report CAO-10-25 Grey County Hybrid Planning Services Delivery Model be
received; and
That council support and communicate to Grey County their in-principle interest in
continued discussions with respect to a hybrid planning service delivery model.
Throughout 2025 and into 2026, Grey County staff have investigated the hybrid planning
services model and developed a draft financial model and memorandum of understanding
(MOU). At the June 11, 2026, County Council meeting, Report PDR-CW-23-26 Hybrid
Planning Services Model Update (attached) was provided. The direction from this report
was to communicate with the municipalities who had indicated in-principle interest and
request confirmation, by resolution of council, as to whether or not the municipality is
committing to the County’s proposed hybrid planning services model or not, subject to
acceptance of a final memorandum of understanding. The County is also seeking the
desired transition timeline should the municipality’s direction be to proceed with the
County’s planning services.
B. Summary of Hybrid Planning Services at the County
1. In-Person Service Delivery
Each participating municipality would specify what level of in-person service delivery they
required. Municipalities would then provide workspace in their municipal offices to
facilitate the in-person service from the County planner at no cost to the County.
2. Defining Core Planning Services
Core planning services are provided to all participating municipalities and would include:
a. Processing planning applications including attending meetings, site visits, writing
reports, pre-submission consultation, and providing recommendations to committees
or council.
b. Preparing official plan and zoning by-law amendments, as well as regular
consolidation of official plans and zoning by-laws.
c. Providing planning advice to municipal council or other municipal departments.
d. Preparing reports to municipal councils on emerging planning matters or legislative /
policy changes.
e. Providing in-person and remote customer service at the agreed upon levels in the
MOU.
f. Assigning a primary planner to each municipality as the ‘go to’ contact for planning
matters between the municipality and the County.
g. Providing evidence at tribunal hearings, in a manner as defined by the MOU.
3. Defining Non-Core Planning Services
Non-core planning services are services that are not provided to all participating
municipalities but may be negotiated as an ‘add on’ service between the County and
municipality (subject to agreement by both parties and appropriate staffing levels). This
includes the following:
a. The creation of new official plans, secondary plans, five or ten-year official plan
reviews, and new comprehensive zoning by-laws.
b. Municipal specific special projects or technical studies (ie. new development charges
background study, various bylaw development or community improvement plan).
c. Drafting legal agreements and legal review of said agreements for subdivisions,
condominiums, site plans, etc.
d. Municipal file creation, file tracking, creating public notices, circulating notices,
mailouts, minute-taking, or drafting meeting agendas for municipal committee or
council meetings, as such responsibilities generally fall to municipal administrative
staff or municipal clerks.
e. Review of non-planning by-laws or permits such as heritage, noise, short-term
accommodation, community improvement plan, etc.
f. Training of municipal staff will be limited. It is the municipality’s responsibility to
provide in-house training on the role and work done by other departments, or those
that directly serve planning in an administrative function.

4. Defining Shared Responsibilities
There are many responsibilities that will fall to both County and municipal staff. These
responsibilities include; data sharing, zoning by-law interpretation, communications,
responding to freedom of information requests, and responding to Ontario Land Tribunal
(OLT) appeals. In the case of the OLT appeals, the MOU spells out what the County staff
involvement would be, versus what remains the responsibility of the municipality.
5. Defining Planning Priorities
The MOU sets out a hierarchy for how planning work is prioritized as follows: (i)
development applications, (ii) legislative changes, (iii) municipal official plan and zoning
by-law updates, and (iv) special projects / studies.
6. Disputes, Disagreements, and Reporting
The MOU sets out a dispute resolution framework. It also sets out a reporting relationship,
whereby the County and a participating municipality would meet a minimum of twice per
year to review operations and receive suggestions for service level adjustments.
7. Other
The MOU sets out that the planners would be County employees, and thus County
Human Resources (HR) and Information Technology (IT) policies would govern staff.
Procurement of specialized expertise on an individual development application, where
needed, would also be governed by the County, with input from the municipality.
Procurement for special projects, e.g., a five-year official plan review would be governed
by municipal processes, with input from County staff where required. The MOU also has
liability, insurance, amendment, and termination clauses, as would be standard for any
such MOU.
C. Town of Hanover Planning Services Overview
Planning and development processes include the following: Zoning By-law Amendment,
Official Plan Amendment, Minor Variance, Consent (Severance) and Plan of Subdivision.
An overview of the steps is as follows:
 Initial contact by phone or in person. Discussion to understand proponent’s goal /
objective and staff advise of the avenue required to move forward.
 Staff advise of the direction following internal pre-consultation meeting that may
involve other Town departments and Grey County representative.
 Application submitted.
 Applicable Planning Act processes implemented (ie notices, Committee of
Adjustment review, public meeting).
 Decision (incudes council decision, conditions/ granting approvals, notice of
decision, appeal timelines).
 Application completed once conditions are deemed met.
The Town processes approximately 25 formal planning applications on an annual basis.
Additionally, we conduct an increasingly large amount of initial contacts and pre-
consultation meetings with perspective developers and landowners in that same period.
These numbers are anticipated to increase as our growth evolves.
Our staffing structure includes one staff role, Junior Planner, with formal planning

Staff Report To Council
From: Melissa Hilgendorff, Human Resources Manager
Date: June 15, 2026
Report: HR-05-26
Subject 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal
Recommendation
That Report HR-05-26 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal be received; and
That council accept the 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal as presented.
Background
Each year our brokers from People Corporation work with Canada Life (CL) to evaluate
the adequacy of the Town’s group benefit plan premiums in relation to the claims paid
and expenses required to operate the program. People Corporation acts on behalf of
the Town to negotiate annual benefit plan renewals, which take effect July 1st of each
year.
Extended Health and Dental benefit rates are set at a level that supports anticipated
claims and expenses for the upcoming year following an analysis of items including the
previous year’s premiums versus claims, administration costs, inflation, and trends.
Basic Life and Long-Term Disability benefits are insured and pooled. Rates are set based
on a blend of the carrier’s ‘manual’ rates, interest rate assumptions, and Town plan
member demographics, including gender, occupation, age, and amount of coverage.
Discussion
Compared to the prior period, the rate of health and vision claims increased by 14.2%
and dental claims increased by 2.0%. Massage, chiropractor, and physiotherapy remain
the top three paramedical services used in the current experience period. The top
medications claimed through the plan provide care for arthritis, glaucoma, and skin
disorders.
To help safeguard against extreme cost increases, once the total health claim amount for
an individual reaches $15,000, the remainder is removed from the Town’s claim
experience and is pooled. Drug claims are most typical of those resulting in pooling. A
total of $42,082 in claims were pooled in the current period which has protected the Town
from larger premium increases.

current and prior renewal periods:

Staff Report To Council
From: Andrew Wilken, Director of Development & Infrastructure/CBO
Date: June 15, 2026
Report: PB-13-26
Subject Revision of Part Lot Control Exemption By-law for 546 and 548 9th Avenue
Recommendation
That Report PB-13-26 Revision of Part Lot Control Exemption By-law for 546 and 548 9th
Avenue be received; and
That council pass By-law No. 3407-26 to remove Part-lot Control from Lot 47, Plan 701,
as described in Parts 1 & 2 on Reference Plan 16R-9761 and Parts 3 & 4 on Reference
Plan 16R-10062, for the purpose of creating two freehold parcels corresponding to the
existing semi-detached dwellings at 546 and 548 9th Avenue; and
That council repeal By-law 3364-25, as the legal description has been updated and
superseded by the current application.
Background
On November 26, 2025, the Town received an application for Part Lot Control under
Section 50(7) of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1990, for the semi-detached dwellings located
at 546 and 548 9th Avenue. The original application referenced Parts 1 and 2 on
Reference Plan 16R-9761, consistent with the 2025 report and By-law 3364-25.
Subsequent review by the applicant’s surveyor and the Town identified that the correct
legal description for the intended freehold parcels also includes Parts 3 and 4 on
Reference Plan 16R-10062. As a result, the original by-law requires replacement to
ensure the proper parts are released from Part Lot Control.
Discussion
The purpose of this Part Lot Control application is to formally separate the two
semi-detached dwelling units at 546 and 548 9th Avenue so that each unit may be
conveyed and owned as an individual freehold parcel. The request does not involve any
construction, redevelopment, or changes to the existing buildings or services. It is a step
to ensure the legal boundaries match the established dividing wall between the two units.
During the review of the original 2025 application, it was determined that the legal
description needed to be updated. The earlier by-law referenced only Parts 1 and 2 on
Reference Plan 16R-9761. Updated survey information confirmed that the correct
description also includes Parts 3 and 4 on Reference Plan 16R-10062. The new By-law
3407-26 incorporates all four parts to reflect the complete and accurate legal description
for registration and future conveyance.
As required by the Planning Act, The by-law will also expire two years after its approval.
Because the updated description replaces the earlier version, By-law 3364-25 is repealed
in its entirety and replaced with the new By-law 3407-26.

BY-LAW NO. 050-06
A By-Law of The Corporation of the Town of Innisfil to regulate the
size, use, location and maintenance of large signs and advertising
devices within the Town of Innisfil.
WHEREAS Council considers it desirable that such a by-law be enacted for all lands within the
corporate limits of the Town of Innisfil; and
WHEREAS Section 99 of the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, c.25 provides Council with the authority to
enact a by-law respecting advertising devices, including signs, and provides Council with the
authority to require compliance with this by-law, and upon default of such compliance, may carry out
such compliance or corrective action as is deemed appropriate and may recover the expenses
incurred in doing so, in like manner as municipal taxes.
NOW, THEREFORE, THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWN OF INNISFIL
ENACTS AS FOLLOWS:
1. This by-law shall be known as The Large Sign By-Law, and shall only be applicable to
billboard signs, ground signs, roof signs and development signs on lands within the
corporate limits of the Town of Innisfil.
2. Definitions
In this by-law:
Billboard Sign means a sign to which advertising copy is fastened, including in such a
manner as to permit its periodic replacement, and which is supported by uprights or braces
embedded in a foundation in or on the ground and which is not attached to any part of a
building, whose principle use is for advertising or displays of goods, products, services or
facilities that are not available at the location of the sign and/or which directs or invites a
person to a location different from that on which the sign is located;
Billboard Sign means an outdoor Sign or Sign that faces outdoors which contains

A message from Heather Dzurko, Manager Waste Management
Date: September 16, 2026
To: Lindsay Ops Public Review Committee
From: Heather Dzurko
Re: Lindsay Ops Annual Monitoring Report Recommendations
Suggested Recommendations:
THAT the Committee receive and accept the 2025 Annual Monitoring Report –
Executive Summary for the Lindsay OPS Waste Disposal Site, attached to this
memorandum;
AND THAT the Committee support the Waste Management Department
proceeding with the 2025 Annual Monitoring Report recommendations to revise
the environmental monitoring program at the Lindsay OPS Landfill Site;
AND THAT staff be directed to work with the City's environmental consultant to
prepare and submit the necessary documentation to the Ministry of the
Environment, Conservation and Parks (MECP) to amend Environmental
Compliance Approval (ECA) No. A321504 to reflect the proposed monitoring
program changes.
Background
The City of Kawartha Lakes is required to undertake environmental monitoring at the
Lindsay OPS Landfill Site in accordance with Environmental Compliance Approval (ECA)
No. A321504. The monitoring program has been in place for more than 40 years and
provides a substantial historical data set from which to assess the site's environmental
performance. Data is provided in the form of an Annual Monitoring Report.
The Lindsay Ops Public Review Committee (PRC) is a forum for the public to evaluate
and make recommendations on decisions respecting the general operations,
environmental monitoring for the Lindsay Ops Landfill Site. The PRC reviews the Annual
Monitoring Report every year as an aspect of their Terms of Reference.
The City's environmental consultant, Azimuth Environmental Consulting Inc. (Azimuth),
completed the 2025 Annual Monitoring Report and reviewed the current monitoring
results in comparison with historical data. The report indicates that the environmental
setting and performance of the Lindsay OPS Landfill Site are well understood based on
the extensive monitoring history. The data continues to demonstrate a relatively
consistent geochemical signature and supports the interpretation that the site is in a
relatively steady-state condition, with no noted off-site contamination concerns.
The 2025 monitoring results also indicate that no trigger mechanism exceedances were
identified. The site met the applicable ECA compliance criteria, with the exception of the
average daily volume of leachate pumped to the Lindsay Water Pollution Control Plant
exceeding the ECA maximum during March and April. Azimuth attributed these
exceedances to increased inputs associated with snow melt events and has
recommended that this continues to be monitored.
Based on the long-term monitoring record and the continued consistency of the
environmental data, Azimuth has again recommended that the City's monitoring
program be reduced and focused on parameters and locations that provide the greatest
environmental value.
These recommendations have been identified in previous annual monitoring reports and
the 2025 results provide continued support for the Azimuth's previous
recommendations. A summary of the proposed changes is outlined below.
Groundwater:
• Remove PCBs (polychlorinated biphenyls) from the list of monitoring parameters
for most groundwater monitors, maintain occasional monitoring (every 3-5
years) in specific bedrock monitors.
• Remove VOCs (Volatile Organic Compounds) from the list of monitoring
parameters.
• Reduce groundwater monitoring from quarterly to semi-annual monitoring,
including groundwater level monitoring.
Leachate:
• Remove PCB, radionuclide, pesticide and VOC from the list of monitoring
parameters.
2
Surface Water:
• Remove PCB and VOC from the list of monitoring parameters at all surface water
locations.
Landfill Gas:
• Focus landfill gas monitoring on locations within or immediately surrounding the
waste mound, given the historical lack of detections throughout the remainder of
the monitoring network.
Wetland Assessment:
• Remove the requirement for a five-year Wetland Assessment, which is currently
scheduled for 2028.
These recommendations are intended to maintain an effective environmental
monitoring program while focusing resources on monitoring locations, parameters and
frequencies that provide meaningful information regarding the site's environmental
performance.
Overview of the Proposed Monitoring Program Changes
Groundwater and Leachate Monitoring
Azimuth noted that decades of sampling for organic priority pollutants (VOCs, PCBs,
pesticides and herbicides, and etc.) have not identified a significant contaminant threat
(AMR Appendix I - reference data in pages 86 to 165).
PCBs are considered relatively immobile in the environment and decades of sampling
have not yielded significant results. Azimuth recommends discontinuing routine PCB
monitoring, with the exception of infrequent sampling at a small number of key
monitoring wells (i.e., 20‐91‐III, 23‐91‐III, 25‐96 & 61‐10‐I) that have identified
leachate influence in the bedrock flow system. These locations would be sampled once
every three to five years.
Decades of monitoring Volatile organic compounds (VOCs) have also not identified
significant results. BTEX concentrations have degraded over time to trace or non-
detectable levels, with only limited and inconsistent trace detections observed at select
locations in 2025 (7-90-II). Based on the historical record, Azimuth noted that
3
continued routine evaluation of these parameters is unwarranted and recommends
discontinue with monitoring for these parameters.
Azimuth also reviewed the historical parameters used to evaluate landfill performance
and recommends focusing the program on parameters that provide a more reliable
indication of landfill-related impacts. Recommendations for additional monitoring
program adjustments are identified below.
• Discontinue phenols monitoring because concentrations have not been
consistently detected and appear to have degraded.
• Discontinue use of phosphorus as a defined landfill indicator parameter due to
inconsistent detections.
• Continue chloride and total ammonia as key landfill indicator parameters.
• Continue monitoring other supporting parameters, including sulphate, iron and
dissolved organic carbon, as recommended in the AMR.
Groundwater monitoring frequency
The consultant has reviewed decades of quarterly groundwater monitoring data and
concludes that changes at the landfill occur slowly and that the system is now
considered to be in a steady-state equilibrium. Based on these findings, the consultant
recommends reducing groundwater monitoring from quarterly to semi-annual
monitoring, including groundwater level measurements. The existing database could be
used to establish normal steady state conditions and if results deviate then quarterly
sampling can resume.
Leachate monitoring and collection system inspections
For leachate sampling, the consultant recommends eliminating, or reducing the
frequency of, PCB, radionuclide, pesticide and VOC analysis due to the historical lack of
detections. The consultant also recommends reducing the frequency of leachate
collection system inspection and flushing to once every three years, or as required
based on operational requirements (AMR Appendix I - reference pages 174 to 181).
Surface Water Monitoring
The purpose of the surface water monitoring program is to assess whether the landfill
has an influence on the adjacent Scugog River and to identify potential contaminant
migration through the site's drainage network. As with groundwater, decades of
sampling have not identified a significant contaminant threat associated with organic
4
priority pollutants (AMR Appendix J - reference pages 49 to 62). Recommendations for
additional monitoring program adjustments are identified below.
• Discontinue PCB monitoring due to the lack of significant historical detections;
• Discontinue VOC monitoring, including BTEX, as concentrations have degraded to
trace or non-detectable levels;
• Discontinue trihalomethane monitoring because these compounds are not
associated with landfill leachate and have only been detected a few times at
trace levels since 2006;
• Continue the current inorganic parameter suite for monitoring locations in the
Scugog River and on-site drainage network.
The recommendations focus on continued surface water monitoring of the inorganic
parameters that are relevant to assessing potential landfill influence while removing
parameters that have not demonstrated value through the historical monitoring record.
Landfill Gas Monitoring
The landfill gas monitoring program is intended to evaluate the potential for landfill gas
migration. Azimuth's assessment indicates that there has been no meaningful landfill
gas migration identified at the site. However, it is recommended that a monitoring
program be maintained as a safeguard and that the frequency be proportionate to the
demonstrated risk. The proposed approach includes the program modifications
identified below.
• Where a monitoring well has shown no detection during the previous five years,
reduce monitoring to an annual late-winter measurement;
• If a detection occurs during annual monitoring, reinstate quarterly monitoring to
confirm the condition and assess whether a trend is developing; and
• Where a monitoring well has shown no detection for 10 years, terminate
monitoring at that location.
This would maintain an ongoing landfill gas safeguard while allowing monitoring
frequency to increase if conditions change.

Dear Solicitor General Kerzner,
I am pleased to submit the 2025 Annual Report of the Inspector General of Policing.
This Report reflects a pivotal year in the continued implementation of Ontario’s modernized
policing oversight framework under the Community Safety and Policing Act (CSPA). In 2025, the
Inspectorate of Policing (IoP) advanced from foundational development to full operationalization of
its mandate—demonstrating how independent, civilian oversight strengthens accountability,
performance, and public trust across Ontario’s policing sector.
A central theme of this year’s Report is legitimacy as the foundation of public confidence in
policing. Our work underscores that legitimacy is not only a function of individual conduct, but of
institutional design—encompassing governance structures, leadership practices, and system-wide
safeguards that shape how authority is exercised and perceived. Legitimate policing is reflected in
actions that are grounded in fairness, transparency, and alignment with the public interest.
Independent oversight plays a critical role in sustaining this legitimacy by providing impartial
scrutiny, reinforcing accountability, and helping to ensure that policing services are delivered and
governed in a manner that maintains public trust. Where legitimacy is strong, consent and
confidence can be sustained; where it is in question, public trust can quickly erode.
Throughout 2025, the IoP exercised its oversight responsibilities through inspections,
investigations, advisory activities, data-driven analysis, and independent research. Notably, we
published Ontario’s first Inspector General Decisions, providing clear, public articulation of
expectations for adequate and effective policing and police governance. These decisions
represent an important step in embedding transparency, clarifying standards, and establishing
precedents to guide the sector.
The Report also identifies a number of ongoing and intensifying challenges impacting policing and
governance across Ontario. Police services and boards continue to operate in an increasingly
complex financial and operational environment, marked by rising costs, expanding responsibilities,
and sustained pressure on municipal budgets. The implementation of the CSPA has also
introduced new legislative and governance requirements, prompting continued adaptation and
capacity-building across the sector.
These pressures are compounded by human resource challenges, including recruitment and
retention pressures, increased workplace absences, and emerging gaps in leadership succession.
At the same time, police services are responding to growing and more complex demands, including
mental health and addictions-related calls, public order events, and evolving community safety
expectations. Governance bodies face parallel pressures, including turnover, vacancies, and the
need for increasingly sophisticated oversight in a rapidly changing environment.
Together, these dynamics underscore the importance of strong governance, clear performance
standards, and effective oversight in ensuring that policing services remain adequate, effective,
and responsive to community needs.
Looking forward, the Report outlines the IoP’s key areas of focus, including the launch of a
province-wide inspection into police integrity and anti-corruption practices. This initiative reflects a
commitment to identifying and addressing systemic risks, and ensuring that Ontario’s policing
institutions remain resilient in the face of emerging challenges.
I would like to express my sincere appreciation to the dedicated professionals of the IoP, whose
expertise, integrity, and commitment have been central to advancing this work. I would also like to
thank police services, police service boards, and community partners across Ontario for their
continued engagement. Advancing effective, accountable, and trusted policing remains a shared
responsibility.

September 9, 2025
City Council
Committee Report
To: Mayor & Council
Fr: Ryan Marsh, Director of Finance
Re: MFOA Request for the Permanent Doubling of the Ontario
Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF) Beyond 2026
Recommendation:
Whereas recent municipal infrastructure funding programs by the Government of Canada
and Province of Ontario have tended to prioritize growth-related or housing-enabling
infrastructure projects over infrastructure renewal needs; and
Whereas the Government of Ontario has regulated municipal infrastructure asset
management through O. Reg 588/17 (Asset Management Planning for Municipal
Infrastructure) under the Infrastructure for Jobs and Prosperity Act, 2015; and
Whereas municipal asset management plans and the Financial Accountability Office of
Ontario have identified that municipalities have significant state-of-good-repair backlogs
and renewal needs for infrastructure; and
Whereas the Government of Ontario doubled the Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund
(OCIF) from $200M/year to $400M/year for 2021-2026 but has not publicly committed
to maintaining this level of funding beyond 2026; and
Whereas the OCIF has become a vital and indispensable resource for municipalities,
assisting them with improving their asset management programs and meeting
community-preserving infrastructure renewal needs; and
Whereas increased geopolitical uncertainty is threatening the economic prosperity of
Canada, Ontario, and every municipality; and
Whereas municipal infrastructure is a key enabler and preserver of economic prosperity;
and
Whereas the Municipal Finance Officers’ Association of Ontario (MFOA) has heard from
its members and their municipalities concerns regarding the potential erosion of existing
municipal infrastructure and thus service levels in light of the ongoing focus on housing-
enabling infrastructure by grant funding programs;
Now Therefore Be it Resolved That the City of Kenora supports MFOA’s letter to the
Ministry of Infrastructure requesting that the doubling of the Ontario Community
Infrastructure Fund be made permanent in advance of the allocations for the 2027
calendar year, helping municipalities to continue building housing-enabling infrastructure
while preserving the economic value provided by existing infrastructure.
Background/Discussion:
To date, 66 municipalities have adopted Council resolutions supporting MFOA's request
that the doubling of the Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF) be made
permanent. OCIF allocations are typically released in the fall, so MFOA is calling for more
municipalities to support this initiative ahead of 2027 allocation announcements.
As a key source of predictable and flexible infrastructure funding, OCIF helps 423 small,
rural, and northern municipalities maintain critical assets, preserve service levels, and
address infrastructure funding challenges identified through asset management
planning.
In June 2026, MFOA submitted a letter (attached) to the Honourable Todd McCarthy,
Acting Minister of Infrastructure, requesting that the Government of Ontario make
permanent the five-year doubling of the Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF)
from $200 million annually to $400 million annually. Acting Minister McCarthy
acknowledged our advocacy efforts in a letter from July 2026, but has not committed to
a permanent doubling of the Fund.
The need for continued and enhanced infrastructure funding is reflected in the City of
Kenora’s 2025 Asset Management Plan developed under Ontario Regulation 588/17. The
Plan identifies municipal infrastructure assets with an estimated replacement value of
$1.41 billion, with 77% of assets assessed to be in fair or better condition. However,
condition assessment data is currently available for only 38% of assets, with the
remaining 62% relying on age-based estimates. Improving asset condition data remains
a key objective of the City's asset management program.
To sustain existing municipal services and prevent the accumulation of future
infrastructure deficits, the Asset Management Plan estimates that the City requires an
average annual capital investment of $29.15 million. Current sustainable funding sources
provide approximately $14.07 million annually, resulting in an estimated annual funding
gap of $15.08 million.
These findings reinforce the importance of maintaining and expanding stable
infrastructure funding programs such as the Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund.
Permanent continuation of the OCIF funding increase would assist municipalities in
addressing state-of-good-repair infrastructure needs, implementing asset management
plans, and reducing long-term pressures on municipal taxpayers.
Budget: The City of Kenora’s 2026 OCIF grant is $2,422,164. Maintaining the current
doubled OCIF funding level beyond 2026 would preserve approximately $2.4 million
annually in predictable infrastructure funding available to support critical infrastructure
renewal projects identified in the City's Asset Management Plan. Continued funding at
this level would help address the City’s estimated annual infrastructure funding gap of
$15.08 million and reduce the burden on property taxpayers.
Risk Analysis: There is minimal risk associated with this report as it is advocacy in
nature and does not commit the City to any financial obligations. Should the Province
discontinue the enhanced OCIF funding level after 2026, the City of Kenora will face
increased challenges in addressing infrastructure renewal needs and funding gaps
identified through asset management planning.
Communication Plan/Notice By-law Requirements: Upon Council approval, a copy
of the resolution will be forwarded to the Honourable Todd McCarthy, Acting Minister of
Infrastructure, Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, Local Member of Provincial
Parliament (MPP), Municipal Finance Officers Association of Ontario (MFOA), Association
of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), Rural Ontario Municipal Association (ROMA) and
Northwestern Ontario Municipal Association (NOMA)

Agenda Item Title: Traffic & Parking Bylaw Amendments – Add No Parking Tow Away
Zone Homestake Rd & Boat Lift Rd, Remove No Parking Tow Away Zone Robertson St
Background Information:
Add No Parking Tow Away Zone - Homestake Rd
The City’s Roads Department has identified safety concerns along a section of Homestake
Road near the Treaty Three Police Service facility located at 22 Homestake Road. Vehicles
are regularly being parked along the north side of the road, creating hazardous conditions
when two vehicles meet and attempt to pass and this is also impeding winter maintenance
operations. Plow trucks and graders are forced to plow around these parked vehicles during
winter snow removal. To address these ongoing concerns, the Roads Department is
requesting no parking on both the North and South sides of the road in this area to alleviate
the ongoing issues.

Add No Parking Tow Away Zone - Boatlift Road
At the start of the 2025 summer season, a paid parking kiosk was introduced at the Boatlift
Road Boat Launch to bring this public launch in line with all other paid City boat launches.
This change prompted a noticeable shift in parking behaviour, leading to an increase in
bylaw complaints about parking congestion in the surrounding area, specifically along
Boatlift Road between the launch parking lot and the CPR tracks at the Portage Bay Bridge.
Vehicles with and without trailers have been observed parking overnight and for extended
periods of time along the sides of Boatlift Road, which is outside the established paid area
while also avoiding the “no overnight parking” restriction associated with the launch’s
parking lot. Overflow parking from Two Bears Marina customers has further compounded
the issue. With the Portage Bay Bridge closure there were times last year that the overflow
parking from the dock rentals were parked right to the bridge and entirely in front of the
jersey barriers currently blocking traffic from going onto the closed bridge. New clear
signage is being erected to help alleviate this congestion on City right-of-way close to the
bridge. Establishing a no parking zone and signage on both sides of Boatlift Road will correct
the undesired parking patterns, easing congestion and supporting safe and unobstructed
emergency vehicle access.

Remove No Parking Tow Away Zone – Robertson Street
The City’s Director of Infrastructure and Operations received a request from a resident on
Guelph Street in Lakeside, for the City to accommodate more on street parking in this
residential area for residents, guests and service vehicles. The City had approved an
amendment November 2024 upon another resident’s request to remove the no parking zone
on Robertson Street from Seventh Street South to Guelph Street for the same reasons and
there have been no issues noted with these changes. Therefore, it was recommended
internally to accommodate the concerns by removing another related section of no parking
on Roberston Street from Guelph Street to the laneway between Guelph Street and Ninth
Street South. The parking restrictions on Robertson Street were historically in place due to
the close proximity of the Ministry building, which was previously accessed by members of
the public for various Provincial government services. This Ministry building is no longer a
service location for the public and hasn’t had full capacity of on-site staff since pre-Covid.
There are no longer traffic or safety concerns in this area that justify the need for the
restriction, and the section of the street is wide enough to accommodate parked vehicles
without obstructing traffic flow or emergency vehicles.

REPORT HIGHLIGHTS:
 The purpose of this report is to provide an update on significant development applications,
policy projects, affordable housing projects and significant projects to streamline and remove
barriers as well as the City’s housing pledge update. Not all work that is currently being
undertaken by the Planning and Housing Policy, and Development and Housing Approvals
Divisions is captured in this report, rather a snapshot of significant work is captured.
 Planning staff provide a quarterly update report every March, June, September, and
December of each year of all current significant development applications. It is important to
provide greater transparency on significant development applications with the community and
Council.
 The key findings of this report include:
o Since signing the Housing Pledge in March 2023, Kitchener Council has approved
Official Plan Amendment and/or Zoning By-law Amendment applications for projects
which propose 18,170 dwelling units (51.9% of housing pledge), Planning staff have
issued final site plan approval for 6,626 dwelling units and building staff have issued
building permits for 9,997 dwelling units.
o Eight initiatives associated with the Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) have received
a Council decision: Growing Together West and Growing Together East;

REPORT:
Since December of 2021, Planning staff have provided a quarterly update report every March,
June, September, and December of all current significant development applications. This report,
and future quarterly reports, include the following:
 Progress and next steps for Kitchener’s Housing Accelerator Fund initiatives;
 Progress and next steps for major planning policy projects;
 A summary of development applications that include affordable housing;
 Housing Pledge reporting - Development application data required to be reported under a
new Provincial regulation – Ontario Regulation 73/23 – Municipal Planning Data Reporting.
Current Significant Development
It is important to provide greater transparency on significant development applications with the
community and Council. Attached to this report, the Significant Planning Applications Quarterly
Report provides a summary of the current Planning applications under review at the time of the
preparation of this report (Attachment A).
The current significant development applications section includes Subdivision, Official Plan
Amendment, and Zoning By-law Amendments that have not received final approval. These are the
bulk of the applications that Planning staff consult with the community on an application specific
basis. Significant development applications include property specific proposals as well as new
greenfield communities (subdivisions). Additional details on the development applications can be
found using the online mapping tool available at www.kitchener.ca/planningapplications.
Kitchener’s Housing Accelerator Fund Initiatives
In November 2023 Kitchener was awarded $42.4 million, payable in 4 annual installments, as part
of the Federal government’s Housing Accelerator Fund to help deliver more affordable housing in
our community. An additional initiative was approved by the Federal Government in March 2025
awarding Kitchener an additional $4.24 million.
Ten action plan initiatives are part of Kitchener’s Housing Accelerator Fund and they include the
delivery of:
 Growing Together West: planning framework updates in Kitchener’s western protected
major transit station areas (COMPLETE);
 Growing Together East: planning framework updates in Kitchener’s eastern protected
major transit station areas (COMPLETE);
 Growing Together West Inclusionary Zoning (COMPLETE);
 Affordable Housing Construction Offset on City-Owned Lands Incentive (IN PROGRESS)
 Not-for-Profit Affordable Rental and Co-op Housing Incentive Pilot (IN PROGRESS);
 Enabling 4 Units – additional dwelling unit implementation (COMPLETE);
 Strategic land acquisition and supporting infrastructure (IN PROGRESS);
 A climate adaptation plan as an input into Kitchener’s new Official Plan (COMPLETE);
 A housing needs assessment (COMPLETE); and,
 Missing Middle and Affordable Housing Community Improvement Plan (IN PROGRESS)
All of the initiatives have either been completed or in progress. The four initiatives in progress will
remain so for the duration of the Housing Accelerator Fund program which concludes later in 2026
as the funding is used for program delivery through financial incentives and strategic land
acquisition. Attachment B provides a description of each initiative, status, next steps and target
completion.

Since 2021 a number of major planning projects have been completed including land use and
zoning updates for all of Kitchener’s protected major transit station areas through Growing
Together East and West; an Inclusionary Zoning Framework; new land use and zoning for the
Hidden Valley and Lower Doon communities; significant progress and completion of the 44 actions
from Housing for All; and the creation and implementation of a Rental Replacement By-law. In

As part of the More Homes for Everyone Act, 2022 (Bill 109), the Planning Act was amended to
give the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing the authority to require municipalities to report
information on planning matters (Section 64). On April 6 2023, the Province implemented Ontario
Regulation 73/23 - Municipal Planning Data Reporting requiring Ontario’s largest and fastest-
growing municipalities, which includes the City of Kitchener, to report development application
information on a quarterly basis (as per Schedule 2 of the regulation) and additional information on
an annual basis (as per Schedule 3 of the regulation).
The data gathered by the Province is being used to measure progress towards various Housing
Supply Action Plan commitments and will also provide the information needed to support informed,
evidence-based decisions around housing and planning policy. The regulation also complements
the Province’s initiative of developing standards and achieving consistency for exchange of data
required for development applications.

Mayor Meloche may move or caused to have moved:
Whereas the Gordie Howe International Bridge represents a significant new international gateway into Windsor-Essex, connecting motorists entering Canada to Highway 401 and the Rt. Hon. Herb Gray Parkway;
And whereas, the Town of LaSalle, a community of more than 36,000 residents, is located immediately adjacent to this important transportation corridor, with direct access from the Rt. Hon. Herb Gray Parkway into our community;
And whereas, current directional signage encountered by motorists entering Canada from the Gordie Howe International Bridge identifies Windsor and Amherstburg, but does not identify the Town of LaSalle;
And whereas, motorists unfamiliar with Windsor-Essex should be clearly informed that the Parkway provides direct access to LaSalle, rather than being directed further into the City of Windsor or to later exits that can take them away from the most direct access to our community;
And whereas, LaSalle's omission from this important gateway signage represents a missed opportunity for wayfinding, tourism and economic development, particularly as the Town continues to develop its waterfront district and attract visitors and investment to our community;
And whereas, appropriate highway signage should accurately identify municipalities and destinations directly accessible from this major international transportation corridor;
Therefore be it resolved that the Council of the Town of LaSalle formally request that the Ontario Ministry of Transportation, in consultation with any other responsible provincial or federal authorities, undertake a review of directional signage for motorists entering Canada from the Gordie Howe International Bridge and travelling onto Highway 401 and the Rt. Background:
A Zoning By-Law Amendment application has been submitted for the vacant property
municipally known by Assessment Roll Number 08-12-812-030-20900-0000. The subject
property is currently zoned Second Density Residential ‘R2’ zone in Township Zoning By-
Law Number 07-079. The ‘R2’ zone permits an apartment dwelling, boarding house, row
house, and triplex dwelling. The purpose of the application is to permit the construction
of an approximately 208 square metre accessory building (garage), which totals 7 metres
in height, in the absence of an established principal residential use on the property. As
per the elevation drawings submitted by the applicant (Exhibit E), the proposed design is
similar to that of a typical residential garage, consistent with the surrounding area. The
proposed amendment would provide site-specific relief from the definition of ‘accessory’
in the Zoning By-Law which specifies that an accessory building or structure is to be

associated with an established principal use. All residential uses in Lansdowne are
required to be connected to municipal water and sanitary services. The subject property
is the last lot within the service area and existing lots to the east of this property are
located outside of the Lansdowne settlement area and are privately serviced lots. The
property subject to this application is not currently serviced and to do so would require an

1) zone is proposed for the property to permit a garage as a primary use, recognize the
location of the proposed structure on the property, and permit an increased maximum
permitted lot coverage for an accessory structure.

Dear Lindsay Lambert:
Re: Application for Minor Variance 45 (1) & Permission 45(2) D13-2026-019
95 Benson Park Road, Township of Leeds and the Thousand Islands
Waterbody: St. Lawrence River
Cataraqui Conservation staff have reviewed the above-noted application and offer the following
comments for the Committee of Adjustment’s consideration. These comments are provided based
on Cataraqui Conservation’s roles as technical advisor to the Township on Planning Act
applications, and as administrator of Ontario Regulation 41/24: Prohibited Activities, Exemptions
and Permits.
Summary of Proposal
Staff understand this application is a combined permission and minor variance application. A
permission is being requested to facilitate the replacement of an existing legal non-complying
dwelling with a new dwelling that has an expanded footprint, floor area and height. The application
is also requesting zoning relief through a variance to permit the following:
- Proposed setback of 15.3 metres from the highwater mark of the St. Lawrence River for a
swimming pool;
- and increase in maximum lot coverage from 10% to 17.3%.
Site Description
The subject property is located on the north shore of Hill Island with approximately 59 metres of
frontage on the St. Lawrence River. The property is approximately 0.36 hectares (0.89 acres) in
size.
The subject property is designated ‘Rural’ and ‘Highly Vulnerable Aquifer’ in the Township’s
Official Plan and is zoned ‘Island Residential’ (IR) in the zoning by-law. The subject lands are also
associated within the 1000 Islands Special Policy Area.
Discussion
The main interest of Cataraqui Conservation with respect to this application is the avoidance of
natural hazards (i.e. flooding and erosion) associated with the St. Lawrence River.
Natural Hazards
Cataraqui Conservation, through our implementation of Ontario Regulation 41/24 and, in
accordance with the natural hazards policies (Section 5.2) of the 2024 Provincial Planning
Statement (PPS), directs development away from lands subject to natural hazards, such as
flooding and erosion to protect people and property.

Flooding
Development and site alteration within and adjacent to the regulatory flood plain is restricted by
Cataraqui Conservation through our implementation of Ontario Regulation 41/24, consistent with
Section 5.2 of the 2024 Provincial Planning Statement.
New flood hazard mapping is now available for the shoreline of Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence
River within Cataraqui Conservation’s jurisdiction (from the Bay of Quinte to just east of
Brockville). The new mapping, which replaces mapping based on a 1994 study, will help inform
responsible decision making for development in or near areas subject to flood risk along the
shoreline. The extent of the regulatory flood hazard at this location along the St. Lawrence
River (1:100 year level plus wave uprush) equates to a 10-metre horizontal offset from the
76 metres GSC elevation.
Based on the provided site plan, a portion of the proposed swimming pool and western extended
patio is located within the safe access component of the flood hazard. New development
(buildings and structure) and site alteration (excavating, grading and placement of fill) is required
to occur outside a minimum 6 metre (safe access) from the regulatory flood hazard. Staff would
request this portion of the site plan be revised to ensure all development (buildings and structure)
and site alteration (excavating, grading and placement of fill) is located outside the minimum safe
access setback (6-metres from the regulatory flood hazard).
Erosion
Development and site alteration within and adjacent to the erosion hazard is also regulated by
Cataraqui Conservation through our implementation of Ontario Regulation 41/24, consistent with
Section 5.2 of the 2024 Provincial Planning Statement. This is typically addressed through the
imposition of appropriate setbacks from the hazard or through mitigation where warranted by site-
specific conditions and the nature of a proposal.
Cataraqui Conservation defines the extent of potential erosion hazards for connecting channels
such as the St. Lawrence River as the sum of either a 1(h):1(v) or 3(h):1(v) slope stability
allowance (depending on slope material), toe erosion allowance, plus an erosion access
allowance of 6 metres. Together, these make up what is known as the ‘Erosion Hazard Limit’.
The entire shoreline is hardened with multi-tiered retaining walls. Based on available information
of the site and adjacent properties, the natural shoreline would consist of exposed granite
bedrock. Since the multi-tiered retaining walls are being maintained, staff do not currently have
concerns relating to the erosion hazard. However, at the permitting stage, staff would request a
structural analysis be completed to determine whether the existing retaining wall structures could
withstand the increased compressive force (new dwelling, expanded patio, pool).
Recommendation
Based on the above information staff would recommend deferral of application D13-2026-019
until the site plan can demonstrate the proposed pool and western extended patio be located
outside minimum safe access setbacks associated with the flood hazard.
Additionally, as noted above, at the permitting stage staff would request a structural analysis be
completed to determine whether the existing retaining wall structures could withstand the
increased compressive force (new dwelling, expanded patio, pool).
