Ministry of the Solicitor General
Dear Solicitor General Kerzner,
I am pleased to submit the 2025 Annual Report of the Inspector General of Policing.
This Report reflects a pivotal year in the continued implementation of Ontario’s modernized
policing oversight framework under the Community Safety and Policing Act (CSPA). In 2025, the
Inspectorate of Policing (IoP) advanced from foundational development to full operationalization of
its mandate—demonstrating how independent, civilian oversight strengthens accountability,
performance, and public trust across Ontario’s policing sector.
A central theme of this year’s Report is legitimacy as the foundation of public confidence in
policing. Our work underscores that legitimacy is not only a function of individual conduct, but of
institutional design—encompassing governance structures, leadership practices, and system-wide
safeguards that shape how authority is exercised and perceived. Legitimate policing is reflected in
actions that are grounded in fairness, transparency, and alignment with the public interest.
Independent oversight plays a critical role in sustaining this legitimacy by providing impartial
scrutiny, reinforcing accountability, and helping to ensure that policing services are delivered and
governed in a manner that maintains public trust. Where legitimacy is strong, consent and
confidence can be sustained; where it is in question, public trust can quickly erode.
Throughout 2025, the IoP exercised its oversight responsibilities through inspections,
investigations, advisory activities, data-driven analysis, and independent research. Notably, we
published Ontario’s first Inspector General Decisions, providing clear, public articulation of
expectations for adequate and effective policing and police governance. These decisions
represent an important step in embedding transparency, clarifying standards, and establishing
precedents to guide the sector.
The Report also identifies a number of ongoing and intensifying challenges impacting policing and
governance across Ontario. Police services and boards continue to operate in an increasingly
complex financial and operational environment, marked by rising costs, expanding responsibilities,
and sustained pressure on municipal budgets. The implementation of the CSPA has also
introduced new legislative and governance requirements, prompting continued adaptation and
capacity-building across the sector.
These pressures are compounded by human resource challenges, including recruitment and
retention pressures, increased workplace absences, and emerging gaps in leadership succession.
At the same time, police services are responding to growing and more complex demands, including
mental health and addictions-related calls, public order events, and evolving community safety
expectations. Governance bodies face parallel pressures, including turnover, vacancies, and the
need for increasingly sophisticated oversight in a rapidly changing environment.
Together, these dynamics underscore the importance of strong governance, clear performance
standards, and effective oversight in ensuring that policing services remain adequate, effective,
and responsive to community needs.
Looking forward, the Report outlines the IoP’s key areas of focus, including the launch of a
province-wide inspection into police integrity and anti-corruption practices. This initiative reflects a
commitment to identifying and addressing systemic risks, and ensuring that Ontario’s policing
institutions remain resilient in the face of emerging challenges.
I would like to express my sincere appreciation to the dedicated professionals of the IoP, whose
expertise, integrity, and commitment have been central to advancing this work. I would also like to
thank police services, police service boards, and community partners across Ontario for their
continued engagement. Advancing effective, accountable, and trusted policing remains a shared
responsibility.
I respectfully submit this Report for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Ryan Teschner
Inspector General of Policing of Ontario

Agricultural Advisory Committee (AAC)
Terms of Reference
Definitions
For the purposes of these Terms of Reference, the following definitions shall apply:
a) “Township” means the Municipal Corporation of the Township of Tay;
b) “Committee” means the Agricultural Advisory Committee;
c) “Council” means the governing body of the Township;
d) “Councillor” means an elected official of the Township, including the Mayor;
e) “Mayor” means the chief elected official of the Township;
f) “Member” means an individual appointed to the Committee;
g) “Municipal Act” means the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended;
h) “Procedural By-law” means the Township By-law which provides the Rules of
Procedure for Council and its Committees.
Purpose
As a Committee of Council, the role of the Agricultural Advisory Committee is to provide
agricultural perspectives related to municipal operations and practices.
Responsibilities
The mandate and responsibilities of the Committee are as follows:
a) Provide input related to the agricultural community;
b) Provide input on the implementation of Provincial and Federal legislation, policies
and guidelines related to the agricultural industry;
c) Provide input on agricultural and rural policy directions pursued by the Township of
Tay. This may include providing advice on municipally initiated official plan
amendments related to agricultural matters, on local agricultural matters through
an official plan review, or other policy directions pursued by the Township;
d) Provide input on the identification and implementation of programs which
encourage public awareness and education of agricultural and related rural issues;
and,
e) Provide input on matters as they arise at the request of Council.
1 | P age
Composition
The Committee shall consist of a minimum of five (5) voting members, being a minimum of
three (3) citizen members from the agriculture community, one (1) Council representative,
and one (1) member who represents the Simcoe County Federation of Agriculture.
Citizen member appointments shall be adopted by Council at the first Regular Council
Meeting of each term.
In accordance with the Township’s Procedural By-law, the Mayor shall be an ex-officio
Member of each Committee and have the same rights as the other Committee Members,
including the right to vote.
Staff representation shall consist of the Municipal Clerk and/or their designate and other
staff resources, as required. Staff shall be non-voting members and shall not be included
to establish quorum. Staff responsibilities as they relate to this committee are limited to
agenda creation and minutes recording, as well as related internal administrative
processes.
Committee members shall be appointed by By-law for the term of Council, four (4) years,
and until their successors are appointed. In the event that a membership vacancy
presents itself during the Term of the Committee, Council shall fill the vacancy by
appointment without the need to advertise.
Chair/Vice-Chair
At its first meeting of each term of office, the Committee shall elect a Chair and Vice-Chair
from among its citizen members. If the role of the Chair becomes vacant for any reason
during a term of office, the Committee shall elect a new Chairperson from among its
citizen members.
The Vice-Chair shall assume the role of the Chair in their absence.
Quorum
A majority of voting members are required to be present to constitute a quorum.
Meetings
The Committee shall adopt the meeting schedule for the year at the first meeting of each
year, if not adopted in the final meeting of the previous year.
The Committee will formally meet two (2) times per year; once in March and once in
November. Additional meetings shall be scheduled as considered necessary by the
Committee or Chair.

If a Member is absent from three (3) consecutive meetings without cause as established
by the Committee, the Chair shall contact the Member in writing to confirm whether they
wish to continue serving on the Committee and commit to the remainder of their term.
Where a Member advises that they no longer wish to serve, or does not respond to the
Chair's written request, the Chair may recommend to Council that the Member be

Meeting Agendas shall be prepared and distributed to all Committee Members prior to

Minutes of all Committee Meetings shall be prepared by the Committee’s Staff Resource
and submitted to Council as part of the next regular Council Agenda.
Resources
The Committee shall request members of management, as well as any other individual as
is deemed appropriate, to participate in Committee Meetings as applicable, so the
Committee may fulfill its responsibilities.
Sub-Committees
The Committee, at its sole discretion, may pass a resolution to appoint sub-committee(s)
on an ad-hoc basis to deal with specific issues relating to its core mandate. A Sub-
Committee so appointed shall produce meeting notes to report to the regular Committee’s
meeting. Appointments to any sub-committee shall be only for the duration of the sub-
committee’s assignment.
For reference purposes, sub-committees are not required for activities within the Purposes
and Responsibilities of the Committee as detailed in this Terms of Reference document.
Reporting
As referenced under the “Meetings” section of this document, the Committee shall report
directly to Council through formal recommendations outlined in meeting minutes, to be
considered at the following regular meeting of Council.

Terms of Reference of the Committee prior to the end of the Council Term and make any
recommendations for amendments prior to the appointment of the new Committee.

Audit Committee (AC)
Terms of Reference
Definitions
For the purposes of these Terms of Reference, the following definitions shall apply:
a) “Township” means the Municipal Corporation of the Township of Tay;
b) “Committee” means the Audit Committee;
c) “Council” means the governing body of the Township;
d) “Councillor” means an elected official of the Township, including the Mayor;
e) “Independent Auditor” means an auditor appointed for the Township as
required by the Municipal Act, 2001;
f) “Internal Controls” means systems, processes, and procedures developed to:
i. Safeguard assets;
ii. Ensure the accuracy of the financial data;
iii. Promote operational efficiency; and
iv. Promote adherence to policies;
g) “Mayor” means the chief elected official of the Township;
h) “Member” means an individual appointed to the Committee;
i) “Municipal Act” means the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended;
j) “Procedural By-law” means the Township By-law which provides the Rules of
Procedure for Council and its Committees.
Purpose
As a Committee of Council, the Audit Committee will be responsible for overseeing all
material aspects of the Township’s financial reporting, control, and audit functions.
The Committee will focus on the qualitative aspects of financial reporting and on the
Township’s processes for the management of financial risk and for compliance with
significant applicable legal, ethical, and regulatory requirements. The Committee provides
a focal point for communication between Council, the independent auditor, and
management, and facilitates an impartial, objective, and independent review of
management practices.
Responsibilities
The Committee shall:
a) Review and assess the annual financial statements before they are brought forward
to Council;

b) Review and assess the key financial statement issues and risks, their impact or
potential effect on reported financial information, the processes used by
management to address such matters, related auditors’ views, and the basis for
audit conclusions;
c) Recommend changes to important accounting principles and the application thereof
in annual financial reports;
d) Review reports from the independent auditors as well as any audit problems or
difficulties and management’s response;
e) Maintain strong, positive working relationships with management, independent auditors
and other advisors.
The Committee may request a report from the Treasurer on matters within its mandate
and within approved budgets.
When the Committee reviews a report it may:
a) Receive it for information;
b) Send it to Council with or without recommendations;
c) Request additional information about matters relating to the report before sending
it to Council with or without recommendations.
Risks and Controls:
Review and assess the Township’s business and financial risk management process,
including the adequacy of the overall control environment and controls in selected areas
representing significant risk.
Review and assess the Township’s system of internal controls for detecting accounting and
financial reporting errors, fraud and defalcations, legal violations, and non-compliance with
the corporate code of conduct.
Review the related findings and recommendations of the independent auditors, together
with management’s responses.
Independent Audits:
Recommend to Council the independent auditor firm to be engaged.
Monitor performance of the independent auditors and ensure that all relevant issues
are reported to the committee.
Obtain a formal written statement from the independent auditors on their independence.
Additionally, discuss with the auditors any relationships or non-audit services that may
affect their objectivity or independence.

Consider, in consultation with the independent auditors, their audit scopes and plans to
ensure completeness of coverage, reduction of redundant efforts, and the effective use of
audit resources.
Review with management and the independent auditors the results of the annual audits
and related comments, including any difficulties or disputes with management, any
significant changes in the audit plans, the rationale behind adoptions and changes in
accounting principles, accounting estimates requiring significant judgments, and the
quality of the accounting principles and financial disclosures adopted.
Review and approve the scope, terms of reference, and fees of professional services

Provide opportunities for private discussion of sensitive matters raised by the independent

c) Ability to understand key business and financial risks and related controls and control

At least one (1) member of the Committee should be literate in business and financial

Committee of Adjustment (COA)
Terms of Reference
Definitions
For the purposes of these Terms of Reference, the following definitions shall apply:
a) “Township” means the Municipal Corporation of the Township of Tay;
b) “Committee” means the Committee of Adjustment;
c) “Council” means the governing body of the Township;
d) “Councillor” means an elected official of the Township, including the Mayor;
e) “Mayor” means the chief elected official of the Township;
f) “Member” means an individual appointed to the Committee;
g) “Municipal Act” means the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended;
h) “Procedural By-law” means the Township By-law which provides the Rules of
Procedure for Council and its’ Committees.
Purpose
The Committee of Adjustment is a statutory tribunal with authority delegated to it by
Township of Tay Council, under the provisions of the Ontario Planning Act, to hold public
hearings to make decisions on applications submitted to the Township’s Planning and
Development Services Department for minor variances, alterations in legal non-
conforming uses and consents or severances. The Committee operates independently
from Council and its decisions may be appealed to the Ontario Land Tribunal. Committee
of Adjustment Members will also sit as a Property Standards Committee to deal with the
Property Standards By-law and will also sit as Fence-viewers to deal with fence matters
under the Line Fences Act.
Committee Mandate
The Committee of Adjustment is a quasi-judicial body, somewhat court-like in its
operation, charged with observance and protection of applicable planning law and also
with protecting the rights of the individuals affected by the decisions made. The common
law principles of natural justice require the Committee of Adjustment to ensure that
individuals affected by their decisions have their equivalent of “a day in court”. The
Committee must also satisfy legal requirements concerning notice, public hearings, calling
of witnesses, notices of decisions and recording of proceedings. As well as the legal
procedures detailed in the Planning Act, the Municipal Act, the Statutory Powers Procedure
Act, the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act and the Municipal Freedom of Information and
Protection of Privacy Act govern the Committee of Adjustment.

The Committee of Adjustment is guided by planning policies and controls established by
the Township of Tay Council through the Township’s Official Plan, the Township’s Zoning
By-law, the County of Simcoe’s Official Plan and Policies approved by the Province of
Ontario.
The goal of the Committee of Adjustment is to provide for and conduct a fair hearing by:
• Allowing anyone wishing to speak to an application an opportunity to do so;
• Giving due diligence to the consideration of each application;
• Openly having all discussions about each application and making all decisions in public
• at the hearing;
• Making rational decisions with appropriate, well-thought-out conditions; and
• Clearly stating the reasons for their decisions.

Purpose
As a Committee of Council, the Grants and Donations Committee shall be responsible for
overseeing and awarding community grants and donations in accordance with the
Township’s Grant and Donations Policy.
Responsibilities
The Committee shall:
a) Review and consider all grant and donation requests;
b) Treat all organizations fairly and consistently so that organizations share available
resources throughout the Township;
c) Provide advice and recommendations regarding the Grants and Donations Policy,
including eligibility criteria, intake, and review process;
d) Recommend grants that meet the requirements set forth in the Grant and Donations
Policy and based on the annual grant budget to Council for consideration;
e) Provide input on matters referred to the Committee by Council that may impact
the Grants and Donation Policy; and
f) Prepare promotional materials to promote the Grants and Donations Program.
Page | 1
Composition
The Committee shall consist of a maximum of three (3) members of Council, with one
non-voting staff representative. Member appointments shall be made by the Mayor at the
beginning of each Council Term.
Staff representation shall consist of the Treasurer and/or their designate and other staff
resources, as required. Staff shall be non-voting members and shall not be included in
establishing a quorum.
Chair/Vice-Chair
At its first meeting of each term of office, the Committee shall elect a Chair and Vice-Chair
from among its voting members. If the role of the Chair becomes vacant for any reason
during a term of office, the Committee shall elect a new Chairperson from among its
voting members.
The Vice-Chair shall assume the role of the Chair in their absence.
Quorum
A majority of voting members are required to be present to constitute a quorum.
Meetings
The Committee shall meet at the call of the Chair.
If a Member is absent from three (3) consecutive meetings and/or events without cause as
established by the Committee, the Chair shall contact the Member in writing to confirm
whether they wish to continue serving on the Committee and commit to the remainder of
their term. Where a Member advises that they no longer wish to serve, or does not
respond to the Chair's written request, the Chair may recommend to Council that the
Member be released from their duties and replaced.
Meeting Agendas shall be prepared and distributed to all Committee Members prior to
each regular meeting, and the business of the Committee shall be taken up in the order in
which it appears on the Agenda.
Minutes of all Committee Meetings shall be prepared by the Committee’s Staff Resource
and submitted to Council as part of the next regular Council Agenda.
Page | 2
Resources
The Committee shall request members of management, as well as any other individual as
is deemed appropriate, to participate in Committee Meetings as applicable, so the
Committee may fulfill its responsibilities.
Reporting
As referenced under the “Meetings” section of this document, the Committee shall report
directly to Council, through formal recommendations outlined in the minutes, to be
considered at the following regular meeting of Council.
The Committee, through the Committee Chair, shall report to Council following the
meeting as to how grant funds were awarded.
The Legislative Services Division, in consultation with the Staff Resource(s), shall review the
Terms of Reference of the Committee prior to the end of the Council Term and make any
recommendations for amendments prior to the appointment of the new Committee.

epidemic in Ontario. Council noted that over 100 municipalities, police services and service providers
across the province are declaring intimate partner violence as an epidemic. Council urges the Province
to immediately pass Bill 173, Intimate Partner Epidemic Act, 2024 to recognize the pervasiveness and
severity of the problem in an effort to stop the violence.

R24-08-350

Violence Epidemic Act, and urges the Province to immediately pass Bill 173 and declare at the
provincial level that Intimate Partner Violence is an epidemic.

Project Information
1. Purpose
The Corporation of the Township of Terrace Bay is seeking quotations for the supply and installation of
a new security camera system to replace its existing dated system.
The Township is seeking a reliable, modern and expandable security camera system that includes all
equipment, software, installation and support required for operation, together with as many priority
cameras as can reasonably be provided within the available project budget. The system must also
allow additional cameras or locations to be added in the future.
2. Project Objectives
The Township’s objectives for this project are to:
• Replace the Township’s dated camera system with a modern digital system;
• Provide a complete and operational system, including all required equipment, software, licensing,
installation and support;
• Replace as many of the Township’s priority existing cameras as reasonably possible within the
available project budget;
• Provide secure and user-friendly access to live and recorded footage;
• Identify any internet, networking and ongoing service requirements associated with the proposed
system; and
• Establish a system that can accommodate additional cameras and municipal locations in the future.
3. Project Locations and Priorities
The current project includes existing cameras at the following municipal locations:
• Terrace Bay Community Centre;
• Terrace Bay Swimming Pool; and
• Simcoe Plaza, where two existing cameras are located.
Priority will be given to replacing the existing cameras at these locations, together with the equipment,
software and infrastructure required to provide a complete and operational system.
One existing outdoor camera operates separately from the system being replaced and can already be
accessed remotely. Replacement or integration of this camera is considered a lower priority and may
be proposed if the available project budget permits.
The final number of cameras replaced will be determined based on the proposed system requirements,
site conditions and available project budget. Proponents may recommend alternative camera
placements where they would provide more effective coverage.
Future expansion to the Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre, Lighthouse or other municipal
locations is addressed in Section 5.
4. Scope of Work
The successful proponent will complete the following work:
• Review the existing camera locations, equipment and site conditions at the Terrace Bay Community
Centre, Terrace Bay Swimming Pool and Simcoe Plaza;
• Recommend an appropriate system design and camera placement;
• Supply and install a complete digital security camera system, including cameras, recording and
storage equipment, software, licensing, cabling, mounts, power supplies and all other required
components;
• Replace or remove existing equipment where required for the new installation;
• Identify any internet connection, networking, subscription, licensing or other ongoing service
requirements and associated costs;
• Configure and test the completed system;
• Provide authorized Township staff with secure access to live and recorded footage;
• Provide system documentation, warranty information and staff training;
• Include as many priority camera replacements as reasonably possible within the available budget
while ensuring the base quotation provides a complete and operational system; and
• Provide a prioritized expansion plan with separately itemized pricing for any priority camera
replacements that cannot be included in the base quotation.
The proposed system must be capable of accommodating additional cameras and municipal locations
without requiring premature replacement of the central recording, storage or management equipment.
5. Optional and Future Services
Proponents may provide separate pricing or planning information for the following:
• Replacement or integration of the newer independently operated outdoor camera;
• Future security camera coverage at the Terrace Bay Cultural Centre, Tourist Information Centre,
Terrace Bay Lighthouse or other municipal locations;
• Public-facing HD livestream coverage at Terrace Bay Beach or the Terrace Bay Lighthouse;
• Livestream capability at the arena for tournaments and events; and
• Livestream capability at the curling club for bonspiels and events.
These items must be identified and priced separately and must not reduce the equipment, installation
or priority camera replacements included in the base quotation. This information is requested for future
planning purposes and may not form part of the work awarded under this RFQ.
6. Site Reference Information
The Township has prepared a Google Earth reference map identifying the existing security camera
locations and providing supplementary site photographs.
For security reasons, access to the map will be provided to proponents upon request. Proponents may
request access by contacting:
Stacy Moffat, Special Projects Coordinator
spc@terracebay.ca
The Terrace Bay Community Centre currently has the following Tbaytel internet services:
• Fibre 1 Gbps service for the Township’s secure office network; and
• 75 Mbps service for free community Wi-Fi.
Proponents must identify whether the proposed system can use either existing connection or requires a
separate dedicated internet service.
The information in this section is provided for reference purposes only. Proponents are responsible for
verifying camera locations, existing infrastructure, site conditions and access requirements.
7. Deliverables
The successful proponent will provide:
• A fully installed and operational digital security camera system, including all required cameras,
recording and storage equipment, software, licensing, materials and other components;
• Configuration and testing of all installed components;
• Secure access to live and recorded footage for authorized Township staff;
• Confirmation of the system’s internet and network requirements, including whether a dedicated
internet service is required;
• System documentation, including camera locations, equipment details, operating instructions,
licensing information and warranty information;
• Training for designated Township staff; and
• A prioritized expansion plan with separately itemized pricing for any priority camera replacements or
future locations not included in the base quotation.
All deliverables must be completed no later than December 11, 2026.
8. Pricing Requirements
Proponents must provide clear, itemized pricing for the base quotation, including:
• Cameras and related equipment;
• Recording, storage and system management equipment;
• Software and licensing;
• Materials;
• Labour and installation;
• Travel and associated expenses;
• Configuration and testing;
• Training; and
• Any other costs required to provide a complete and operational system.
Proponents must also identify:
• Any internet, networking or connectivity requirements and associated one-time or recurring costs;
• Any licensing, subscription, maintenance or other recurring costs;
• Separate pricing for any priority camera replacements not included in the base quotation;
• Separate pricing or planning information for the optional and future services identified in Section 5;
and
• Warranty coverage and the cost of any optional extended warranty or support services.
The Township has an available 2026 project budget of $15,000, excluding HST, and is seeking a
complete and operational system within or as close as reasonably possible to this amount.
All pricing shall be provided in Canadian dollars.
9. Submission Requirements
Proponents shall provide:
• Relevant experience and qualifications;
• Proposed system design and approach;
• The number, type and proposed location of cameras included in the base quotation;
• Details regarding recording, storage, system access and future expansion capacity;
• Proposed project timeline;
• Warranty and post-installation support information;
• A prioritized expansion plan for cameras or locations not included in the base quotation;
• References for at least two comparable projects; and
• Completed pricing information in accordance with Section 8.
10. Evaluation
Submissions will be evaluated based on:
• Relevant experience and qualifications;
• Understanding of the project scope;
• Proposed system and approach;
• Equipment, coverage and overall value provided within the available budget;
• Capacity for future expansion; and
• Cost.
The Township is not obligated to accept the lowest-priced submission and may select the submission
that provides the best overall value.
11. General Conditions
The Township reserves the right to:
• Accept or reject any or all submissions;
• Request clarification or additional information from any proponent;
• Adjust the final combination of cameras and locations in consultation with the preferred proponent,
based on the available budget; and
• Cancel this RFQ without awarding a contract.

North Shore Compliance Audit Committee
The Compliance Audit Committee is an independent statutory body that reviews and decides on
applications for audits of municipal election campaign finances. The municipalities of Terrace Bay,
Marathon, Manitouwadge and Schreiber are currently seeking qualified individuals to serve as members
on the North Shore Compliance Audit Committee (NSCAC) for the 2026 Municipal Election.
Who should apply:
Applications are encouraged from individuals with experience in:
• Law and investigations • Compliance, governance
• Accounting or auditing • Public administration
• Finance • Municipal government
Under the Municipal Elections Act, 1996, municipal employees and officers, members of council or
local boards, election candidates, and registered third parties are not eligible to serve on the North
Shore Compliance Audit Committee.
What Does a Compliance Audit Committee Do?
The Compliance Audit Committee reviews and makes decisions regarding applications for
compliance audits of campaign finances for Council candidates and registered third party advertisers
in municipal elections and by-elections. The committee can:
• Determine whether an elector’s application for a compliance audit should be granted or rejected
• Appoint a qualified auditor if an application is approved
• Receive and reviewing the auditor’s report
• Decide whether legal proceedings should be initiated where a contravention appears to have
occurred
• Determine whether audit costs should be recovered from the applicant if no contravention is found
and the application lacked reasonable grounds
The Committee also reviews reports from the Clerk identifying contributors who may have exceeded
contribution limits and determines whether legal action should be considered.
Committee Information
• The Compliance Audit Committee will be composed of 5 members, ideally including one member
from each of the participating communities, depending on qualifications
• The term of appointment will extend through the 2026 Municipal Election and conclude on
November 14, 2030.
• Committee members will receive remuneration and reimbursement in accordance with the
applicable municipal policy or agreement.

BACKGROUND
The subject property is a single ownership island located within the Sans Souci – Copperhead
Neighbourhood in the Official Plan. The property has a lot area of approximately 2.86 ha and is
developed with two modest main dwellings, a boathouse, two docking sites and accessory
structures. The property is zoned Coastal/Island Residential Exception 17 (CR-17). The
current site-specific zoning is the result of a past Zoning By-law Amendment application and
decision of the Ontario Municipal Board (now known as Ontario Land Tribunal). The decision
of the OMB permitted the property to be developed with two 100 m2 single detached dwellings,
two boathouses and other permitted accessory buildings and structures. The intent is to
separate the two existing detached dwellings, however, based on the neighbourhood growth
policies, an Official Plan Amendment is required.
2
PUBLIC MEETING SUMMARY
A public meeting was held on June 19, 2026. The agent, Mr. Jonathan Pauk of Morgan
Planning & Development, and the owners attended. No members of the public attended or
submitted comments. Council asked the agent and township staff questions about the proposal
and raised preliminary concerns that future development of accessory buildings could exceed
what is currently permitted under the existing zoning. In response to the concerns raised, the
applicants have amended the original proposal to reduce the number of accessory buildings
being proposed, see the attached letter submitted by the agents, which summarizes the revised
proposal. The revised proposal no longer increases the number of accessory buildings.
PLANNING ANALYSIS
1. PROVINCIAL PLANNING STATEMENT
The subject property is located within a rural area as per Section 2.5 of the Provincial Planning
Statement, 2024 (PPS). Section 2.6 of the Provincial Planning Statement recognizes limited
residential development and resource-based recreational activities on the subject property, it
states:
2.6.1. On rural lands located in municipalities, permitted uses are:
b) resource-based recreational uses (including recreational dwellings not
intended as permanent residences);
c) residential development, including lot creation, where site conditions are
suitable for the provision of appropriate sewage and water services;
Further, Section 2.6.2. of the Provincial Planning Statement states:
2.6.2. Development that can be sustained by rural service levels should be promoted.
The existing dwellings are both currently serviced by their own separate septic systems.
Natural Heritage
Policy 4.1 of the PPS addresses Natural Heritage, specifically regarding significant wetlands,
significant wildlife habitat, significant areas of natural and scientific interest, fish habitat and
habitat of endgames and threatened species.
In accordance with relevant environmental policies, the applicants submitted an Environmental
Impact Study, completed by Terrastory Environmental Consulting Inc. in support of the
applications. The conclusion of the study supports the proposal, provided the recommendations
and mitigation measures are implemented to achieve “no negative impact”. This includes
3
recommendations related to timing windows for vegetation removal, erosion/sediment control
measures and setbacks from Type 1 Fish Habitat (wetlands) and shoreline. The conclusions
of the report are based on minimal additional development on the island, with continued
limitations on the maximum dwelling’s sizes of 100 m2 and one additional boathouse. The
Environmental Impact Study does not appear to include the development of additional
accessory buildings, which was permitted per the original Ontario Municipal Board decision and
has been proposed to be carried forward in the Zoning By-law Amendment.
Below is an excerpt from the Environmental Impact Study, which maps the biophysical and
natural heritages features identified on the property.

The revised proposal essentially distributes the existing development rights between the two
proposed lots and no longer results in any additional buildings being permitted. As a result, the
revised proposal appears to be consistent with the recommendations within the Environmental
Impact Study of no new development.
2. OFFICIAL PLAN
Section 10 of the Official Plan establishes Neighbourhood Growth Policies, which are effectively
land division policies for the various areas in the Township. Schedule ‘A’ to the Official Plan
identifies the subject lands as being located within the Sans Souci Copperhead Neighbourhood.
The relevant policies applicable to this Neighbourhood include the following:
4
“10.29 Sans Souci – Copperhead Neighbourhood contains one of the most heavily
travelled waterways in The Archipelago. Development is either concentrated in pockets
such as Sans Souci or is sparse in other areas and the status quo should be maintained
as far as possible to preserve the rich heritage of this area.
This neighbourhood is heavily influenced by the presence of The Massasauga Provincial
Park. In recognition of the Park extra care will be taken by the Township in its review of
building and development applications.
There are several large land holdings that may be considered for development so long
as strict controls are applied to promote conservation in this area.
10.30 Further land division in the Sans Souci Copperhead Neighbourhood is to be
discouraged. A consent involving the creation one new lot per land holding greater than
five hectares may be considered subject to Section 14 – Development Procedures and
Standards. Consents involving the creation of up to two new lots per land holding may
be considered by the Township on parcels greater than ten hectares subject to Section
14 – Development Procedures and Standards. Land holdings greater than fifteen and
twenty hectares may qualify for land division resulting in the creation of up to three or
four new lots per land holding respectively subject to Section 14 - Development
Procedures and Standards and any other applicable policies.’
The above policy requires a minimum lot area of 5 hectares (12.35 ac) to be eligible for
consideration of the creation of one new lot. As the subject property has a lot area of 2.86
hectares, hence, an Official Plan Amendment is required. The development policies are
intended to maintain the current character of the neighbourhood, ensuring development is
appropriate. As the subject property will not be permitted any additional development, the
proposal would maintain the status quo and will not result in any additional development.
Rather, the proposal will facilitate the two existing dwellings to be transferred independently.
In addition, Section 14.49 of the Official Plan states:
‘14.49 Wherever land division policies allow for consents for the creation of new lots in
the various neighbourhoods (except for the Pointe au Baril Station
Neighbourhood), and minimum lot standards are not identified, the minimum lot
size will be 100 m of water frontage and 1 hectare of lot area. These numerical
figures are not absolute and may in appropriate circumstances be varied slightly
to accommodate individual applications.’
The proposal will result in lots both with a lot area of 1.43 hectares and a lot frontage of 133.5
metres and 143.3 metres. As a result, both would conform to policy 14.49 of the Official Plan.
5
Section 14.9 of the Official Plan states:
’14.9 It is the policy of this Plan that only one dwelling is allowed on one parcel of land.
However, a second dwelling is permitted on a lot where the lot is eligible for a
land division provided that the resulting location of the second cottage would
meet the criteria for severance at some future point including suitable location for
docking facilities.’
The proposal will result in each lot having a single detached dwelling, which conforms with the
above policy.

Subject: Water Access Task Force Term Report
The Water Access Task Force (WATF) was established by Council at the June 17, 2022
meeting of Council.
The Township of The Archipelago Official Plan recognizes that marinas and other water access
facilities are essential for providing access and services to residents and visitors, and that they
make important contributions to local economies. Further, through the Official Plan, the
Township supports marinas and will work with business owners, local residents and other levels
of government such that water access facilities remain available to the residents of the
Township.
The Federation of Cottager’s Associations had published a Report on the declining number of
marinas in the Province and the potential impact that might have on water access. This
coincided with resident discussions with Councillors about the potential impact of marina
conglomerates, monopolies, and service for contractors.
The WATF initially did a scan of water access across the Township by Ward to identify the
current status of water access and to identify potential concerns (see Appendix A). A legal
opinion was also solicited regarding the factors affecting Township decision-making. Further,
the background and Official Plan Amendment of a previous Taskforce were reviewed (see
Appendix B).
During that review, it was determined that Blackstone Lake needed attention in cooperation with
the Blackstone Lake Cottagers’ Association (BLCA). A series of consultations and
investigations followed.
CONCLUSION & RECCOMENDATIONS
1. Many of the issues identified by both BLCA and Angler’s Marina have been addressed
between the Parties such that the urgency for action on other options has quieted.
2. It still remains that Blackstone Lake has only one Access Point.
3. The WATF recommends to Council that the TOA should consider options to ensure
water access where necessary, including the purchase of vacant or private land, a
marina or a right of first refusal, should the opportunity arise.
4. That Council for the Township of The Archipelago receive and endorse the August
report.

Context
The Nation Municipality is experiencing significant growth, particularly in the western
regions, leading to increased demands on municipal services. To ensure that the
municipality can continue to meet these demands while preparing for future challenges,
a comprehensive HR Action Plan has been developed. This plan addresses leadership
development, job role clarity, compensation and benefits, and succession planning, all
aimed at building a resilient and capable workforce.
Report
The HR Action Plan 2025-2028 is designed to address the key challenges and
opportunities facing The Nation Municipality’s human resources. The plan focuses on
four main initiatives:
1. Workforce Planning and Staffing Adjustments: Ensuring the right staffing
levels and skills to meet service demands.
2. Leadership and Professional Development: Building a strong leadership
pipeline and enhancing staff capabilities.
3. Job Role Clarity and Organizational Structure: Aligning roles and
responsibilities with strategic objectives for greater efficiency.
4. Succession Planning and Knowledge Transfer: Preparing for key retirements
by ensuring smooth transitions and knowledge retention.
These initiatives are strategically phased to align with the municipality's growth and
budgetary considerations, ensuring The Nation remains resilient and capable of
delivering high-quality services to its residents.

This HR Action Plan aligns with common priorities in municipal government, such as
sustainable growth, operational efficiency, and delivering high-quality services. By
investing in our workforce, The Nation is positioning itself to effectively meet the

region.

Attendance in June 2026 totalled 2,753 visitors compared to 2,180 visitors in June 2025, representing an
increase of 573 attendees or 26.3 percent. The increase was driven largely by strong attendance during
TurtleFest, which continues to be one of the community's most significant annual events. Donation visitor
attendance increased from 1,594 visitors in June 2025 to 1,909 visitors in June 2026, an increase of 315
attendees or 19.8 percent. During TurtleFest, Annandale National Historic Site welcomed 416 visitors on
June 19 and 1,364 visitors on June 20.
Paid visitation more than doubled, increasing from 94 visitors in June 2025 to 203 visitors in June 2026. This
growth was supported by increased general visitation throughout the month, including a tour group of 54
visitors. June also marked the introduction of a new school program connected to the Annandale Farm: A
Model Farm exhibition. Three Grade 3/4 classes participated in the program, generating 106 student visits
and providing students with an opportunity to learn about local agricultural history.
Programming attendance decreased from 55 participants in June 2025 to 13 participants in June 2026. This
change reflects the introduction of school programming in place of some public programming offerings, as
well as lower attendance for the workshop on offer in June. Rental attendance increased from 150 attendees
to 242 attendees, reflecting increased use of the site for private rentals.
Attendance in July 2026 totalled 2,735 visitors, down from 3,028 in July 2025, a decrease of 293 attendees
or 9.7 percent.
Paid visitation rose from 141 visitors in July 2025 to 479 visitors in July 2026, an increase of 338 visitors or
239.7 percent. This increase was largely driven by a visit from the Model T Ford Club, which included 304
visitors to Annandale NHS in a single day. The annual tour visits a different region each year, and
Annandale NHS was selected as a 2026 tour stop. Staff and volunteers played a key role in welcoming
visitors and supporting site operations during the visit. Paid visitation for July excluding the tour participants,
would have totaled 175 visitors, exceeding July 2025 attendance levels.
Programming attendance also increased significantly, rising from 61 participants in July 2025 to 109
participants in July 2026, an increase of 78.7 percent. This growth is attributed to increased registration in
summer camp programming. Staff believe that the introduction of expanded drop-off and pick-up times,
aligned with those offered at the Tillsonburg Community Centre, provided greater flexibility for families and
contributed to higher participation.
Rental attendance decreased from 872 attendees in July 2025 to 482 attendees in July 2026. While the
Tillsonburg and District Historical Society's Music on the Lawn series continued to be well attended,
individual event attendance was lower than the previous year.
Attendance in August 2026 totaled 1,082 visitors compared to 1,596 visitors in August 2025, a decrease of
514 attendees or 32.2 percent. The most significant change was in rental attendance, which declined from
1,035 attendees in August 2025 to 205 attendees in August 2026. This decrease is largely attributable to
three cancellations of the Tillsonburg and District Historical Society's Music on the Lawn series due to
inclement weather.
Despite the decline in overall attendance, several categories experienced growth. Paid visitation increased
from 171 visitors to 219 visitors, reflecting continued growth in site visitation. Programming attendance rose
from 127 participants to 140 participants. Membership attendance increased from 45 visits to 76 visits,
supported in part by volunteers assisting with summer camps and community events.
Community and operational attendance increased from 218 visits in August 2025 to 354 visits in August
2026. This increase is primarily attributable to guardians accompanying children to summer camp drop-off
and pick-up periods. Donation visitor attendance increased from zero in August 2025 to 88 attendees in
August 2026, attributable to attendance at the When the Cows Come Home festival.

reached 9,178 visitors compared to 8,876 visitors during the same period in 2025, representing an increase
of 302 attendees or 3.4 percent.
Programming
Programming activity throughout late June, July, and August focused on seasonal events, summer camps,
community outreach, and community partnerships.
Annandale National Historic Site participated in TurtleFest on June 19 and 20, offering a variety of family-
friendly activities and educational experiences. Friday evening activities included turtle-themed
programming, a movie on the lawn, and food trucks. On Saturday, the site hosted lawn games, a scavenger
hunt throughout the museum, educational activities in partnership with Scales Nature Park, and LEGO-
based activities. TurtleFest continues to be a significant community event and remains an important
opportunity to introduce new audiences to the museum.
July began with the Canada Day Open House and Fun Fair, which welcomed visitors for a day of family-
friendly activities and community celebration. Staff would like to extend their appreciation to the volunteers
and museum staff whose support contributed to the success of the event.
Four weeks of summer camp programming were delivered throughout July and August. Themes included
Canada Welcomes the World; Life on the Farm; Adventures Unlimited; and Ticket to Ride. Camp registration
exceeded the previous year and contributed significantly to overall programming attendance during the
reporting period.
A post-camp survey was distributed to participating families to gather feedback on the 2026 summer camp
season. Survey collection remains ongoing; however, responses received to date have been
overwhelmingly positive. All respondents indicated they were satisfied with the overall camp experience,
with the majority reporting they were "Very Satisfied" with camp staff, communication, daily scheduling, and
the sign-in/sign-out process. Families also reported high levels of camper engagement, with respondents
consistently indicating that campers felt positively engaged with camp leaders, fellow participants, and the
camp environment.
Written feedback highlighted the quality of camp staff, the variety of activities offered, and the themed camp
experiences as program strengths. Several families identified the museum's camp as their child's favourite
camp experience of the summer, while others expressed interest in additional camp weeks being offered in
future years. Staff will continue to collect feedback and review survey results to support future program
development and operational planning.

Re: Federal Bill C-15, the ALTO High-Speed Rail Project, and Municipal Interests
Please be advised that the Council of the Township of Tyendinaga passed the following
resolution at their regular meeting August 12, 2026:
Resolution: 231-2026
Moved by: Councillor Jen Phillips
Seconded by: Deputy Mayor Lang
WHEREAS the Council of the Township of Tyendinaga has previously passed
resolutions expressing concerns regarding the Alto High-Speed Rail Project and
Bill C-15;
AND WHEREAS Council has stated that it does not support the project as presented
due to its potential impacts on residents, farmland, the environment, municipal
infrastructure and property rights;
AND WHEREAS the recently announced consideration of a route serving Kingston,
including the possibility of an alignment along or near Highway 401, would not
eliminate these concerns but could create significant adverse impacts in another
area of Tyendinaga Township;
AND WHEREAS this area contains homes, productive farmland and Tyendinaga
Public School, the only public school located within the Township, serving nearly
400 students;
AND WHEREAS Tyendinaga Township is a wholly rural municipality whose
residents rely heavily on access to the urban centres of Belleville and Napanee for
employment, shopping, health care and other essential services, with three
Highway 401 interchanges and an additional overpass currently supporting that
access;
AND WHEREAS Old Highway 2, the principal alternative route to Belleville and
Napanee, is located south of Highway 401 and could also become inaccessible to
affected residents if crossings through the potential rail corridor are closed,
restricted or altered;
AND WHEREAS the resulting loss or restriction of access to Highway 401 and Old
Highway 2 could significantly affect residents, school transportation, emergency
response and access to area hospitals;
AND WHEREAS the project’s estimated cost of $60 billion to $90 billion is
preliminary and cannot be properly evaluated before the route, required
infrastructure, environmental and geological challenges, property acquisition costs
and impacts on municipal infrastructure and services are known;
AND WHEREAS proceeding with a project of this scale without a defined route,
dependable cost estimate and clear accounting of its full financial implications
presents a significant risk to Canadian taxpayers;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Council of the Township of

The Corporation of the Municipality of Tweed
Staff Report
Date: August 11, 2026 Council Meeting
Report to: Council
Report from: Cindy Chow, Manager, Community Development, Parks & Rec
Department: Community Development
Title: Backyard Hen Program - Background Report
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this report is to provide Council with background information regarding
backyard hen programs and to summarize regulations currently in effect in several
Ontario municipalities. The report is intended for Council's consideration of a potential
Backyard Hen Program within the Municipality of Tweed and to seek direction regarding
the development of a draft by-law and regulatory framework for future Council review.
BACKGROUND:
Staff have received inquiries from residents regarding the keeping of backyard hens for
personal egg production. A growing number of Ontario municipalities permit backyard
hens while establishing regulations intended to address animal welfare, public health,
biosecurity, neighbourhood compatibility, property maintenance, and enforcement
requirements.
Benefits of backyard hens:
 Supports local food production and food security.
 Provides educational opportunities for families and youth.
 Encourages self-sufficiency and sustainable living practices.
 Aligns with Tweed's rural character and agricultural heritage.
 May contribute to waste reduction through composting of approved organic
materials and responsible manure management.
Challenges of backyard hens:
 Potential noise and odour complaints.
 Attraction of pests, rodents, and predators.
 Disease and biosecurity concerns, including Avian Influenza.
 Animal welfare considerations.
 Compatibility concerns within residential neighbourhoods.
 Additional municipal administration, enforcement, and oversight requirements.
Review of municipal backyard hen programs indicates several common
regulatory provisions:
 Roosters are generally prohibited.
 Most municipalities limit the number of hens permitted.
 Backyard hens are intended for personal use only.
 Coops and runs are required to meet setback and construction standards.
 Coop size and height restrictions are commonly established.
 Manure management and sanitation requirements are required.
 Property owners are responsible for cleanliness, maintenance, and animal care.
 Building, Planning, and Municipal Law Enforcement staff typically play a role in
implementation and enforcement.
 Most municipalities utilize a complaint-based enforcement model.

POTENTIAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE MUNICIPALITY OF TWEED
Should Council direct staff to prepare a draft by-law, the following framework could be
considered:
 Maximum of six (6) hens per residential property.
 Roosters prohibited.
 Home slaughter is prohibited.
 Breeding is prohibited.
 No commercial egg production or sales.
 No commercial agricultural operation.
 No ducks, geese, turkeys, guinea fowl, peafowl, or other poultry species.
 Rear-yard coop placement only.
 Minimum setbacks from lot lines and neighbouring dwellings.
 Compliance with zoning, property standards, and animal welfare requirements.
 Secure storage of feed and bedding materials.
 Proper disposal of deceased birds in accordance with applicable regulations.
 Complaint-based enforcement model.
 Potential licensing or permit requirements subject to further review.
Zoning Considerations
Staff will review whether backyard hens should be permitted as an accessory residential
use and identify any necessary zoning restrictions, including permitted areas, minimum
lot sizes, and setback requirements for coops and runs.
Licensing Considerations
Council may wish to consider a licensing system to support education, compliance
tracking, and enforcement. Without licensing, enforcement would be primarily
complaint-driven.
Building and Coop Requirements
Staff will consult with Building Services regarding permit requirements, size and height
restrictions, construction standards, and predator protection measures for coops and
runs.
Property Standards and Nuisance Control
A backyard hen by-law should address manure management, odour, pests, waste
storage, and general property maintenance to prevent nuisance conditions.
Animal Welfare
Minimum standards should include access to food and water, adequate shelter and
ventilation, protection from predators, and appropriate coop and run sizes.
Avian Influenza and Biosecurity
Staff will review applicable biosecurity practices, disease prevention measures, and any
provincial guidance related to avian influenza.
Predator Control
Requirements may include secure feed storage, predator-resistant coops, enclosed
runs, overnight confinement of hens, and proper waste management to reduce wildlife
attraction.
Enforcement Considerations
The effectiveness of a backyard hen program depends largely on having clear,
enforceable regulations. A complaint-based enforcement model is generally appropriate
because:
 Proactive inspections are resource intensive;
 Routine inspections are generally unnecessary;
 Most complaints involve odour, sanitation, noise, rodents, predators, or excessive
numbers of hens.
Potential enforcement tools may include:
 Written warnings;
 Orders to Comply;
 Administrative Monetary Penalties, where applicable;
 Licence suspension or revocation, if licensing is implemented; and
 Removal orders.
Noise
While roosters can be prohibited, hens are not entirely silent.
 Any excessive noise generated by backyard hens would remain subject to the
Municipality's Noise By-law, where applicable.
Consultations
Prior to preparation of a draft by-law, staff recommend consultation with:
 Building Services;
 Planning and Zoning;
 Municipal Law Enforcement;
 Southeast Public Health Unit;
 Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness, or other applicable provincial
agricultural authority;
 Local veterinarians, where appropriate; and local agricultural organizations, where
appropriate.
These consultations will assist staff in developing recommendations respecting zoning,
lot sizes, setbacks, coop requirements, biosecurity, licensing, animal welfare standards,
administration, and enforcement.
OPTIONS:
1. Direct staff to undertake further consultation and prepare a draft Backyard
Hen By-law for Council consideration.

Purpose
To request Council approval of the amendments to the Toronto and Region Assessment
Report (Assessment Report), as well as the Credit Valley, Toronto and Region, Central
Lake Ontario Source Protection Plan (Source Protection Plan). Under the Clean Water
Act, 2006, municipal endorsement of the proposed amendments is required prior to
formal submission to the Ministry of Environment, Conservation and Parks for review
and approval.
Report Highlights
 Source water protection is regulated by the Clean Water Act, 2006 and is
critical to ensuring clean and safe drinking water from surface and
groundwater sources.
 Amendments to the Assessment Report and Source Protection Plan are
required to reflect the addition of Nobleton Well 6, the increase in water taking
and the new delineation of the Nobleton Wellhead Protection Area (WHPA).
 The amended Assessment Report and Source Protection Plan enable
mitigation of potential drinking water quality and quantity threats and the
continued protection of municipal drinking water through local Official Plans
and Zoning By-laws.
 As the new Nobleton Wellhead Protection Area delineation extends into a
small area of North Vaughan, the proposed amendments require Municipal
Council endorsement to proceed through the Ministry of Environment,
Conservation and Parks approval process.

Background
Source Water Protection
“Source water” refers to untreated water found in rivers, lakes, and underground
aquifers that is used as raw water supply for municipal drinking water systems. Source
water protection involves the measures taken to safeguard these water sources from
contamination and overuse, ensuring the long-term safety and sustainability of drinking
water resources. The Clean Water Act, 2006 mandated the establishment of localized
Source Protection Authorities responsible for developing, implementing, and
maintaining Source Protection Plans and Assessment Reports.
Source Protection Plans and Assessment Reports
The Source Protection Plan contains a suite of policies that drive action and
management practices to protect the quality and quantity of source water. These
management policies are activated through local Official Plans and Zoning By-laws to
ensure significant drinking water threats are not enabled through land use or
development activities.
The Toronto and Region Assessment Report, Toronto and Region Source Protection
Authority, Version 6.0, March 2024 (Assessment Report) identifies areas in York Region
that require focused efforts to protect source water by delineating vulnerable areas and
evaluating specific activities that may pose a threat to drinking water resources. As part
of these focused efforts, Wellhead Protection Areas are generated which create a
designated area around municipal extraction wells where specific land use policies
apply to mitigate risks to source water. The size of the Wellhead Protection Area is
determined by a computational model that estimates groundwater travel times based on
pumping rates and the specific hydrogeologic conditions of the subsurface.
A key requirement under the Clean Water Act, 2006 is that these documents remain
current as municipal drinking water systems evolve. This includes updating Assessment
Reports and Source Protection Plans whenever new drinking water sources, such as
newly constructed extraction wells, are added to a municipal water supply system. The
Toronto and Region Source Protection Authority is responsible for updating or

to Section 34 of the Clean Water Act, 2006, the councils of affected municipalities are
required to endorse proposed amendments prior to their submission to the Ministry of

reliability of the community’s water supply. To align with the recommendations provided,
York Region drilled and constructed Nobleton Well 6 and amended the associated
Permit to Take Water to accommodate increased water taking and planned growth.

2. APPLICATION
2.1 Unless a separate by-law has been passed setting out a specific procedure to
be followed for a Committee, in all proceedings of Council and its Committees,
the following rules and regulations shall apply and be observed and shall be the
rules and regulations for the order and dispatch of the business in Council and
the Committees thereof:
(a) Parliamentary Authority
All matters, Points of Order or questions of procedure arising and not
provided for in the rules contained herein shall be in accordance with
“Meetings Procedures, Parliamentary Law and Rules of Order for the 21st
Century” by James Lochrie.
(b) Distribution of this By-law
Following a regular or new municipal election, the Clerk shall provide each
Member with a copy of this by-law, including amendments thereto.
(c) Amendments to this By-law
No amendment, alteration or addition to this by-law shall be made unless
due notice has been given setting forth the proposed amendment,

alteration or addition at a previous Meeting and a majority of all Members
present vote thereon.
(d) Food and Beverages at Meeting
Consumption of beverages, other than water, and the consumption of food
shall not be permitted in the Council Chambers during a Meeting.
(e) Electronic Devices
All cell phones, pagers, radios, etc. shall be switched off, non-audible or
muted during a Meeting with the exception of pagers and similar devices
carried by members of the fire service or other first responders, in the
interest of public safety.
3. CONFLICT OF INTEREST
3.1 Members are required to comply with the provisions of the Municipal Conflict of
Interest Act, R.S.O. 1990, c.M.50, as amended.
3.2 Disclosures of Interest
3.2.1 Where a Member, either on his or her own behalf or while acting for, by, with or
through another, has any Pecuniary Interest, direct or indirect, in any matter and
is present at a Meeting of the Council or local board at which the matter is the
subject of consideration, the Member:
a) Shall understand and comply with their legal obligations under the
prevailing conflict of interest legislation;
b) Shall, prior to any consideration of the matter at the Meeting, disclose the
interest and the general nature thereof;
c) Shall not take part in the discussion of, or vote on any question in respect
of the matter; and
d) Shall not attempt in any way whether, before, during or after the Meeting
to influence the voting on any such question
3.2.2 At a Meeting in which a Member discloses an interest, or as soon as possible
afterwards, the Member shall file with the Clerk, a written statement of the
interest and its general nature on the form prescribed by this By-law (attached
as Schedule “A”)

4. NOTICE OF MEETINGS
4.1 The schedule of Regular Meetings of Council shall be posted to the Township’s
website annually upon Council approval.
4.2 Notice of a Regular Meeting and all Meetings for public information shall consist
of posting of an Agenda of the said Meeting on the Township’s website, at least
three (3) days prior to the date of the Meeting.
4.3 Notice for public information of a Special Meeting shall be posted as soon as
practical with the intent of Section 4, taking into account the overriding
provisions of Subsections 5.4 and 5.5 herein.
4.4 The Township shall give notice for specific items of public interest to be
considered at Meetings, in accordance with its Notice Policy.
4.5 Any Amendments to the Agenda shall be made available to the public as soon
as is practicable prior to the Council meetings by posting the Amendment on the
Township website.
5. GENERAL ORDER OF PROCEDURES AT COUNCIL
5.1 Location
All Meetings shall be held in the Council Chambers at the Municipal
Administration Building, 31940 Highway #3, Wainfleet, unless otherwise
established in advance by resolution of Council.
5.2 Inaugural Meeting
The Inaugural Meeting after a regular election and a by-election under Section
226 (1) of the Municipal Elections Act shall be held at 7:00 p.m. on the first
Tuesday following the date of the commencement of the term of the new
Council. The opening ceremonies for the Inaugural Meeting shall be as
determined by the Clerk.
5.3 Regular Meetings
5.4 Regular Meetings shall be held in the Council Chambers at the Municipal
Administration Building every third Tuesday at 6:30 p.m. in accordance with the
Council meeting schedule prepared by the Clerk and approved by Council
resolution, unless Council, by resolution, directs otherwise.

5.5 Special Meetings
(a) The Mayor may at any time summon a Special Meeting.
(b) The Clerk shall, upon receipt of a written petition signed by a majority of
the Members, summon a Special Meeting for the purpose and at the time
and place mentioned in the petition.
(c) The Clerk shall provide all Members and the public with a minimum of
forty-eight (48) hours’ notice of all Special Meetings.
(d) Minimum notice to all Members shall consist of a telephone message
and/or email followed by a written notice and Agenda by email.
(e) The only business to be dealt with at a Special Meeting is that which is
identified in the notice of the Meeting.
(f) The lack of receipt of a notice or an Agenda for a Special Meeting by any
Member shall not affect the validity of the Meeting or any action taken
thereat.
5.6 Emergency Meetings
(a) Notwithstanding any other provision of this by-law, an Emergency Meeting
may be summoned by the Mayor to deal with an emergency or other
extraordinary situation, as determined by the Mayor in her or his sole and
unfettered discretion.
(b) The Clerk shall notify or attempt to notify all Members and the public about
the Emergency Meeting as soon as possible and in the most expedient
manner available, including, but not limited to, posting a notice on the
Township’s website.
(c) No business except business dealing directly with the emergency or
extraordinary situation shall be transacted at the Emergency Meeting.
(d) The lack of receipt of a notice or an Agenda for an Emergency Meeting by
any Member shall not affect the validity of the meeting or any action taken
thereat.
5.7 Recording and Live Streaming
(a) Regular Meetings shall be recorded electronically and, when possible,
shall be broadcast by live stream on youtube.com. At the discretion of the
Clerk in consultation with the Mayor, Special Meetings of Council may be
recorded electronically and, when possible, broadcast by live stream on

impair the ability of the Township to broadcast via live stream, the
Township shall endeavour to record the proceedings electronically and

(b) Signage shall be posted in Council Chambers to ensure that presenters
and members of the public are aware that the Meeting proceedings are

(Councilor Lee)
  WHEREAS, homelessness, mental health, and substance use disorders continue to represent a growing public health and community safety crisis across Niagara, including within the City of Welland; and
WHEREAS, municipalities are increasingly managing the direct impacts of these crises through emergency response, by-law enforcement, community safety, shelter pressures, and local services, placing growing strain on municipal and healthcare resources; and
WHEREAS, individuals experiencing homelessness, mental health challenges, and addictions frequently require access to crisis stabilization, withdrawal management, complex care, recovery supports, and integrated health services; and
WHEREAS, gaps in local and regional treatment capacity contribute to increased emergency department utilization, hospital strain, EMS offload delays, and ongoing pressures on frontline services; and
WHEREAS, the Province of Ontario has identified mental health and addictions as priority areas for investment and healthcare system transformation; and
WHEREAS, the Niagara Health Welland Hospital site is currently undergoing planning and redevelopment consideration through a provincially supported planning process; and
WHEREAS, meaningful collaboration between municipalities, healthcare partners, social service agencies, and individuals with lived and living experience can strengthen long-term community outcomes.
NOW THEREFORE LET IT BE RESOLVED THAT THE COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF WELLAND formally declares homelessness, mental health, and substance use to constitute a municipal and public health emergency requiring coordinated action across all levels of government; and
THAT the City of Welland calls upon the Ontario Ministry of Health and Niagara Health to ensure the ongoing planning and future redevelopment of the Welland Hospital site includes consideration for expanded:
- mental health and addictions treatment services;
- withdrawal management and stabilization capacity;
- complex continuing care and recovery beds; 
- integrated community-based health supports; and
THAT the City of Welland requests that municipal perspectives, local service impacts, and community-based healthcare needs be incorporated into the ongoing planning and business case development process for the future of the Welland Hospital site; and further
THAT this resolution be circulated to the Minister of Health, local MPPs, Niagara Region, Niagara Health, and Niagara-area municipalities for their consideration.   Ref. No. 21-30

Dear City Clerk and Members of Council,
We, the parents and next of kin of Carrie Lynn Pinard, hereby submit this formal letter of
support and consent in accordance with the City of Welland’s Facility Naming Policy. This
submission is provided to support the naming of the Dain City new school’s dedicated
community space in honour of our daughter, Carrie Lynn Pinard, and includes background and
biographical information demonstrating her significance to the local community.
Carrie was raised in the City of Welland, specifically within the Dain City community, where
she lived, attended school, and developed strong personal and community ties. Dain City was
Carrie’s home throughout her formative years, and it remains the community most closely
connected to her life and legacy. The proposed facility is located within this same community,
establishing a clear and meaningful geographic and historical connection.
Carrie attended Bridgeview School from kindergarten through Grade 8. During her time there,
she was well known and well respected by peers, educators, and community members. She later
continued her education at the secondary level, carrying forward the values instilled through her
upbringing in Welland—kindness, generosity, and respect for others.
At the age of 18, Carrie’s life was tragically and senselessly taken as a result of gun violence
while she was in Toronto. She was an innocent victim, in the wrong place at the wrong time. Her
death had a profound impact on her family, friends, and the Welland community and extended
beyond the municipality, contributing to broader public awareness and dialogue related to gun
violence, the young offenders act and community safety. Carrie’s story became part of the
momentum supporting changes to gun legislation in Canada, reflecting the wider social
significance of her legacy.
At the time of her passing, Carrie was working part-time as a model and had just been accepted
to attend the University of Toronto. Carrie was known for her confidence, determination, and
positive spirit. She was widely regarded as kind, generous, and compassionate, with a warm
smile and genuine care for others. She was a loving and devoted sister to her two sisters and a
cherished daughter. Carrie was admired not only for her outward beauty, but for her character
and the way she treated those around her.
In recognition of Carrie’s life and the impact of her story, the recreation gym at the former
Bridgeview School, which has been leased by the City of Welland since 1994, was previously
named the Carrie Lynn Pinard Community Memorial Centre. That naming reflected the
community’s desire to acknowledge both Carrie’s connection to Welland and the lasting
significance of her legacy. The facility served as a space for recreation, inclusion, and
community gathering, and its name became associated with remembrance, safety, and collective
responsibility.
As the City undertakes the development of a new school and dedicated community space to
address the needs of Dain City’s growing population, we respectfully request that this established
recognition be carried forward. Naming the new community space in honour of Carrie Lynn
Pinard would preserve continuity, reflect the historical significance already recognized by the
City, and maintain a meaningful connection between the facility and the community it serves.
On behalf of our family and friends, we formally provide our full consent and support for the
naming of the new school’s dedicated community space in honour of Carrie Lynn Pinard. We
appreciate the City of Welland and it’s Council, their consideration of this request and its
commitment to recognizing individuals whose lives and legacies hold lasting significance within
the community.
Sincerely,
Bob and Margaret Pinard

2. Purpose:
The Planning and Development Department is in receipt of an application for a
Zoning By-law Amendment for the subject land. The purpose of this report is to
present information related to the application at a statutory public meeting, as
required by the Ontario Planning Act.
3. Background:
3.1. Site and Area Description
The subject land is located south of Mary Street East and is bounded by
Ash Street and Hickory Street North. The subject land is municipally
known as 303, 305, and 307 Mary Street East and 150 Hickory Street
North (refer to Attachment #1). The subject land is approximately 0.37 ha
(0.92 acres) in size.
The subject land is currently occupied by one (1) vacant building at 307
Mary Street East and one (1) residential dwelling at 150 Hickory Street
North. Surrounding land uses include the following:
 A 6-storey apartment building (Whitby Village Senior Housing) to
the north;
 An auto sales and auto body shop to the east;
 A 6-storey residential building and single-detached dwellings along
Hickory Street North to the south; and,
 Low-rise single detached residential dwellings to the west (refer to
Attachment #2).
Report PDP 45-26
Public Meeting Page 3 of 6
3.2. Application and Proposed Development
A Zoning By-law Amendment Application has been submitted by MHBC
Planning Limited on behalf of Cosmopolitan Homes Mary Street Inc. to
develop four, 4-storey stacked townhouse blocks, comprising a total of 48
units (refer to Attachment #3).
The proposed development includes 1.25 parking spaces per unit and 12
visitor parking spaces.
The Zoning By-law Amendment Application proposes to change the
current zoning from H-R6-DT and H-R5-DT within Zoning By-law No. 2585
to an appropriate zone category to accommodate the proposed
development.
A future Site Plan Application and Draft Plan Subdivision will be required
to create the block for a future common-element condominium.

4. Discussion:
4.1. Envision Durham Official Plan
The subject land is designated as Regional Centre on Map 1 – Regional
Structure in the Envision Durham Official Plan. Regional Centres are
intended to be hubs for culture, services shopping, and key to the identity
of their broader surrounding communities and are planned for a built form
mix of contextually appropriate high-rise and mid-rise development,
providing an appropriate transition in building height, density and massing
to surrounding areas, and with a mix of uses and public spaces that
provide for complete and vibrant communities.
